title: Joshua

stories.title: 🌊 Joshua 1
summaryBullets: Now after the death of His servant Moses, the LORD spoke to Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ assistant, saying, (1:1).
“Moses My servant is dead. Now therefore arise, you and all these people, and cross over the Jordan into the land that I am giving to the children of Israel. (1:2).
I have given you every place where the sole of your foot will tread, just as I promised to Moses. (1:3).
Your territory shall extend from the wilderness and Lebanon to the great River Euphrates— all the land of the Hittites— and west as far as the Great Sea. (1:4).
No one shall stand against you all the days of your life. As I was with Moses, so will I be with you; I will never leave you nor forsake you. (1:5).
Be strong and courageous, for you shall give these people the inheritance of the land that I swore to their fathers I would give them. (1:6).

Above all, be strong and very courageous. Be careful to observe all the law that My servant Moses commanded you. Do not turn from it to the right or to the left, so that you may prosper wherever you go. (1:7).

This Book of the Law must not depart from your mouth; meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do everything written in it. For then you will prosper and succeed in all you do. (1:8).
Have I not commanded you to be strong and courageous? Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.” (1:9).
Then Joshua commanded the officers of the people: (1:10).

“Go through the camp and tell the people, ‘Prepare your provisions, for within three days you will cross the Jordan to go in and take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.’” (1:11).
But to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, Joshua said, (1:12).
“Remember what Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you when he said, ‘The LORD your God will give you rest, and He will give you this land.’ (1:13).

Your wives, your young children, and your livestock may remain in the land that Moses gave you on this side of the Jordan. But all your mighty men of valor must be armed for battle to cross over ahead of your brothers and help them, (1:14).

until the LORD gives them rest as He has done for you, and your brothers also possess the land that the LORD your God is giving them. Then you may return to the land of your inheritance and take possession of that which Moses the servant of the LORD gave you on the east side of the Jordan.” (1:15).
So they answered Joshua, “Everything you have commanded us we will do, and everywhere you send us we will go. (1:16).
Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you. And may the LORD your God be with you, as He was with Moses. (1:17).
Anyone who rebels against your order and does not obey your words, all that you command him, will be put to death. Above all, be strong and courageous!” (1:18).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 31:1-8: Moses charges Joshua in the sight of all Israel to be strong and courageous, for the LORD goes with him.
Deuteronomy 34:1-12: Moses views the land from Nebo and dies in Moab, and Joshua is full of the spirit of wisdom.
Numbers 32:20-32: Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh promise to cross over armed ahead of their brothers.
Deuteronomy 11:24-25: Every place the sole of your foot treads shall be yours, from the wilderness to the Euphrates.
Psalm 1:1-3: His delight is in the law of the LORD, and on His law he meditates day and night.

translationNotes.term: All the land of the Hittites
translationNotes.note: The Hittites ran an empire out of Anatolia, in what is now Turkey, and fought Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh on the Orontes. For a long stretch of the nineteenth century they were known from no source but the Bible. Their capital Hattusa, at Boghazkoy in central Turkey, was excavated from 1906 under Hugo Winckler, who found the royal cuneiform archives, including the empire's own copy of the treaty with Egypt.

translationNotes.term: From the wilderness and Lebanon to the Euphrates
translationNotes.note: The four limits are real geography. The wilderness is the dry Negev and Sinai to the south, Lebanon is the mountain range to the north, the Euphrates is the great river running down through Syria to the north-east, and the Great Sea is the Mediterranean on the west. Genesis 15:18 gave Abraham the same frame, from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates.

translationNotes.term: Meditate on it day and night
translationNotes.note: Hagah is a noise word. It is used of a lion growling over its kill (Isaiah 31:4) and of a person moaning like a dove (Isaiah 38:14). Reading in this world was normally done out loud, which is why the same verse says the book must not depart from your mouth. The instruction is to keep muttering it over, not to sit and think quietly.

A sepher is a scroll. Sheets of leather or papyrus were sewn end to end and rolled, written in columns, and read by unrolling with one hand while rolling up with the other; bound books with pages did not exist yet. Torah means instruction or direction, from a root meaning to point the way, so the phrase is closer to the scroll of instruction than to a law code.

translationNotes.term: The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh
translationNotes.note: These two and a half tribes had already been given land east of the Jordan by Moses, because the grazing there suited their herds, on the condition that their fighting men cross over armed and stay in the field until every other tribe had its land (Numbers 32:1-33). Verses 12 to 15 are Joshua calling in that agreement, and Joshua 22 is them finally going home. The word for armed here, chamushim, is the same one used of Israel marching out of Egypt in ranks in Exodus 13:18.

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD commissions Joshua to lead Israel across the Jordan into the promised land, assuring him of divine presence and victory; Joshua orders the people to prepare for departure and reminds the eastern tribes to fight alongside the others before returning to their own territory.

stories.title: 🌊 Joshua 2
summaryBullets: Then Joshua son of Nun secretly sent two spies from Shittim, saying, “Go, inspect the land, especially Jericho.” So they went and entered the house of a prostitute named Rahab and stayed there. (2:1).
And it was reported to the king of Jericho: “Behold, some men of Israel have come here tonight to spy out the land.” (2:2).
So the king of Jericho sent to Rahab and said, “Bring out the men who came to you and entered your house, for they have come to spy out the whole land.” (2:3).
But the woman had taken the two men and hidden them. So she said, “Yes, the men did come to me, but I did not know where they had come from. (2:4).
At dusk, when the gate was about to close, the men went out, and I do not know which way they went. Pursue them quickly, and you may catch them!” (2:5).
(But Rahab had taken them up to the roof and hidden them among the stalks of flax that she had laid out there.) (2:6).
So the king’s men set out in pursuit of the spies along the road to the fords of the Jordan, and as soon as they had gone out, the gate was shut. (2:7).
Before the spies lay down for the night, Rahab went up on the roof (2:8).
and said to them, “I know that the LORD has given you this land and that the fear of you has fallen on us, so that all who dwell in the land are melting in fear of you. (2:9).

For we have heard how the LORD dried up the waters of the Red Sea before you when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to Sihon and Og, the two kings of the Amorites across the Jordan, whom you devoted to destruction. (2:10).
When we heard this, our hearts melted and everyone’s courage failed because of you, for the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below. (2:11).
Now therefore, please swear to me by the LORD that you will indeed show kindness to my family, because I showed kindness to you. Give me a sure sign (2:12).
that you will spare the lives of my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and all who belong to them, and that you will deliver us from death.” (2:13).
“Our lives for your lives!” the men agreed. “If you do not report our mission, we will show you kindness and faithfulness when the LORD gives us the land.” (2:14).
Then Rahab let them down by a rope through the window, since the house where she lived was built into the wall of the city. (2:15).
“Go to the hill country,” she said, “so that your pursuers will not find you. Hide yourselves there for three days until they have returned; then go on your way.” (2:16).
The men said to her, “We will not be bound by this oath you made us swear (2:17).

unless, when we enter the land, you have tied this scarlet cord in the window through which you let us down, and unless you have brought your father and mother and brothers and all your family into your house. (2:18).

If anyone goes out the door of your house into the street, his blood will be on his own head, and we will be innocent. But if a hand is laid on anyone with you in the house, his blood will be on our heads. (2:19).
And if you report our mission, we will be released from the oath you made us swear.” (2:20).
“Let it be as you say,” she replied, and she sent them away. And when they had gone, she tied the scarlet cord in the window. (2:21).
So the spies went out into the hill country and stayed there three days, until their pursuers had returned without finding them, having searched all along the road. (2:22).
Then the two men started back, came down from the hill country, and crossed the river. So they came to Joshua son of Nun and reported all that had happened to them. (2:23).
“The LORD has surely delivered the entire land into our hands,” they said to Joshua. “Indeed, all who dwell in the land are melting in fear of us.” (2:24).
crossRefs: Hebrews 11:31: By faith Rahab did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given the spies a friendly welcome.
James 2:25: Rahab was justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way.
Matthew 1:5: Rahab is named in the line of Judah as the mother of Boaz.
Exodus 15:14-16: The peoples have heard and tremble; terror and dread fall on the inhabitants of Canaan.
Deuteronomy 20:16-18: In the cities of these nations you shall save alive nothing that breathes.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה (ishah zonah) - Greek: πόρνη (porne)
translationNotes.note: Verse 1 calls Rahab a zonah, the ordinary Hebrew word for a prostitute, and the New Testament keeps it, calling her the porne at Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25. Her house stood against the town wall, at the edge of Jericho where strangers came and went and where two unknown men lodging for a night drew no comment. Matthew 1:5 lists her by name in the line that runs down to David.

The camp Joshua sends the spies out from, on the plains of Moab east of the Jordan opposite Jericho, named for the acacia trees that grow in that dry country. Numbers 33:49 gives the fuller name, Abel-shittim, and places Israel's camp along the river there. It is also where Israel joined in the worship of Baal of Peor with Moabite women and twenty-four thousand died in the plague that followed (Numbers 25:1-9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תִּקְוַת חוּט הַשָּׁנִי (tiqvat chut ha-shani) - תּוֹלַעַת שָׁנִי (tolaat shani)
translationNotes.note: Shani is crimson dye, taken from the dried bodies of a scale insect that lives on the kermes oak; the fuller Hebrew name for it, tolaat shani, means worm of scarlet. It was costly, and it is the same red yarn listed for the tabernacle curtains and the high priest's garments (Exodus 25:4, 28:5-6). A cord in that colour hanging from a window would still be visible after weeks of siege, which is what verse 18 requires of it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פִּשְׁתֵּי הָעֵץ (pishtei ha-ets), stalks of flax
translationNotes.note: Verse 6 has Rahab hide the men under stalks of flax laid out on the flat roof. Flax was pulled in spring, soaked, then dried in the sun before the fibres could be beaten out and spun into linen, and a roof was the standard drying floor. The scarlet cord she is given in verse 18 is the same trade: she is a woman with linen and rope in the house.

translationNotes.term: Her house was in the wall
translationNotes.note: Verse 15 says the house was built into the town wall, so she could let the men down on the outside by a rope from the window. Canaanite towns were small and cramped, and building living quarters into the casemate wall was ordinary use of space. It also puts her at the edge of the town in every sense, which is why the spies end up there.

stories.keyTakeaway: Joshua sends two spies to scout Jericho; they hide at Rahab's house, and she protects them from the king's soldiers in exchange for a promise that she and her family will be spared when Israel conquers the land. The spies report back that the people of Jericho are afraid and the Lord has given the land into Israel's hands.

stories.title: 🌊 Joshua 3
summaryBullets: Early the next morning Joshua got up and left Shittim with all the Israelites. They went as far as the Jordan, where they camped before crossing over. (3:1).
After three days the officers went through the camp (3:2).
and commanded the people: “When you see the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God being carried by the Levitical priests, you are to set out from your positions and follow it. (3:3).
But keep a distance of about two thousand cubits between yourselves and the ark. Do not go near it, so that you can see the way to go, since you have never traveled this way before.” (3:4).
Then Joshua told the people, “Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you.” (3:5).
And he said to the priests, “Take the ark of the covenant and go on ahead of the people.” So they carried the ark of the covenant and went ahead of them. (3:6).
Now the LORD said to Joshua, “Today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, so they may know that I am with you just as I was with Moses. (3:7).
Command the priests carrying the ark of the covenant: ‘When you reach the edge of the waters, stand in the Jordan.’” (3:8).
So Joshua told the Israelites, “Come here and listen to the words of the LORD your God.” (3:9).

He continued, “This is how you will know that the living God is among you and that He will surely drive out before you the Canaanites, Hittites, Hivites, Perizzites, Girgashites, Amorites, and Jebusites. (3:10).
Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth will go ahead of you into the Jordan. (3:11).
Now choose twelve men from the tribes of Israel, one from each tribe. (3:12).

When the feet of the priests who carry the ark of the LORD — the Lord of all the earth — touch down in the waters of the Jordan, its flowing waters will be cut off and will stand up in a heap.” (3:13).
So when the people broke camp to cross the Jordan, the priests carried the ark of the covenant ahead of them. (3:14).
Now the Jordan overflows its banks throughout the harvest season. But as soon as the priests carrying the ark reached the Jordan and their feet touched the water’s edge, (3:15).

the flowing water stood still. It backed up as far upstream as Adam, a city in the area of Zarethan, while the water flowing toward the Sea of the Arabah (the Salt Sea) was completely cut off. So the people crossed over opposite Jericho. (3:16).

The priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firm on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan, while all Israel crossed over the dry ground, until the entire nation had crossed the Jordan. (3:17).
crossRefs: Exodus 14:21-22: The LORD drives the sea back and Israel goes over on dry ground, the waters a wall on their right and left.
Psalm 114:3-5: The sea looked and fled; the Jordan turned back; what ails you, O Jordan, that you turn back?
Numbers 4:15: The Kohathites carry the holy things on their shoulders, and must not touch them, or they die.
Deuteronomy 31:7-8: The LORD Himself goes before you; He will not leave you or forsake you, so do not fear.
2 Kings 2:8,14: Elijah and then Elisha strike the water of the Jordan with the rolled cloak and cross over on dry ground.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וַיַּעַמְדוּ הַמַּיִם (vayyaamdu ha-mayim), the waters stood
translationNotes.note: Verse 16 says the water coming down stood still and rose up in one place, while the water running toward the Salt Sea was cut off completely. The verb is amad, to stand, the same picture as Exodus 14:22, where the sea is a wall on the right and the left. The text does not say the river ran low that year; it says the water stood.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֵד אֶחָד (ned echad), one heap
translationNotes.note: Ned is a rare word for water piled up and holding its shape. Exodus 15:8 uses it of the Red Sea, where the floods stood upright in a heap, and Psalm 78:13 repeats it. Joshua 3:16 is reaching for the vocabulary of the earlier crossing on purpose.

Verse 16 does not just say the river stopped; it says where. The water stood still a long way upstream at a town called Adam, beside Zarethan, near the mouth of the Jabbok. That is roughly eighteen miles north of the crossing opposite Jericho, so the text is telling the reader how much riverbed was left dry.

Verse 15 notes the Jordan overflows all its banks throughout the harvest. Barley is cut in March and April, which is exactly when the snow melting off Mount Hermon runs down and fills the river. Israel crosses at the one season of the year when the fords are useless and an army has no way over.

Verse 4 sets the people about two thousand cubits behind the ark, roughly a thousand yards, and tells them not to come near it. The gap is practical as well as reverent: everyone in a column that long can see where the ark is going, since none of them has been this way before.

stories.keyTakeaway: Joshua leads Israel from Shittim to the Jordan; officers instruct the people to follow the ark of the covenant, and Joshua tells them to consecrate themselves. The priests carrying the ark enter the flooded Jordan and the water stops flowing, allowing all Israel to cross on dry ground while the priests stand in the riverbed.

stories.title: 🌊 Joshua 4
summaryBullets: When the whole nation had finished crossing the Jordan, the LORD said to Joshua, (4:1).
“Choose twelve men from among the people, one from each tribe, (4:2).

and command them: ‘Take up for yourselves twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan where the priests were standing, carry them with you, and set them down in the place where you spend the night.’” (4:3).
So Joshua summoned the twelve men he had appointed from the Israelites, one from each tribe, (4:4).

and said to them, “Cross over before the ark of the LORD your God into the middle of the Jordan. Each of you is to take a stone upon his shoulder, according to the number of the tribes of Israel, (4:5).
to serve as a sign among you. In the future, when your children ask, ‘What do these stones mean to you?’ (4:6).

you are to tell them, ‘The waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD. When it crossed the Jordan, the waters were cut off.’ Therefore these stones will be a memorial to the Israelites forever.” (4:7).

Thus the Israelites did as Joshua had commanded them. They took up twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan, one for each tribe of Israel, just as the LORD had told Joshua; and they carried them to the camp, where they set them down. (4:8).
Joshua also set up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan, in the place where the priests who carried the ark of the covenant stood. And the stones are there to this day. (4:9).

Now the priests who carried the ark remained standing in the middle of the Jordan until the people had completed everything the LORD had commanded Joshua to tell them, just as Moses had directed Joshua. The people hurried across, (4:10).
and after everyone had finished crossing, the priests with the ark of the LORD crossed in the sight of the people. (4:11).
The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh crossed over before the Israelites, armed for battle as Moses had instructed them. (4:12).
About 40,000 troops armed for battle crossed over before the LORD into the plains of Jericho. (4:13).
On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and they revered him all the days of his life, just as they had revered Moses. (4:14).
Then the LORD said to Joshua, (4:15).
“Command the priests who carry the ark of the Testimony to come up from the Jordan.” (4:16).
So Joshua commanded the priests, “Come up from the Jordan.” (4:17).

When the priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD came up out of the Jordan and their feet touched the dry land, the waters of the Jordan returned to their course and overflowed all the banks as before. (4:18).
On the tenth day of the first month the people went up from the Jordan and camped at Gilgal on the eastern border of Jericho. (4:19).
And there at Gilgal Joshua set up the twelve stones they had taken from the Jordan. (4:20).
Then Joshua said to the Israelites, “In the future, when your children ask their fathers, ‘What is the meaning of these stones?’ (4:21).
you are to tell them, ‘Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground.’ (4:22).
For the LORD your God dried up the waters of the Jordan before you until you had crossed over, just as He did to the Red Sea, which He dried up before us until we had crossed over. (4:23).
He did this so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, and so that you may always fear the LORD your God.” (4:24).
crossRefs: Exodus 12:26-27: When your children ask what this rite means, you shall say, it is the sacrifice of the LORD's Passover.
Deuteronomy 6:20-25: When your son asks the meaning of the testimonies, you shall tell him we were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt.
Exodus 13:14-16: When your son asks what this means, you shall say the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a strong hand.
Joshua 24:26-27: Joshua sets a great stone under the oak as a witness, because it has heard all the words the LORD spoke.
Genesis 28:18-22: Jacob sets up the stone he had slept on as a pillar, pours oil on it, and calls the place Bethel.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָה הָאֲבָנִים הָאֵלֶּה (mah ha-avanim ha-elleh)
translationNotes.note: Verses 6, 21 and 22 build the monument around a question a child will ask and supply the answer to be given back. The same pattern runs through the law: Exodus 12:26 and 13:14 for the Passover, Deuteronomy 6:20 for the commandments. Teaching was spoken, and it worked by set question and set answer, so twelve stones by the road are a prompt for a lesson, not an ornament.

translationNotes.term: The tenth day of the first month
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֶּעָשׂוֹר לַחֹדֶשׁ הָרִאשׁוֹן (be-asor la-chodesh ha-rishon)
translationNotes.note: Verse 19 dates the crossing exactly. The first month is Abib, later called Nisan, falling in March or April, and the tenth day of it is the day Exodus 12:3 sets for taking the Passover lamb into the house. Four days later, on the fourteenth, Israel keeps the Passover at Gilgal (5:10).

Verse 16 switches the name from ark of the covenant to ark of the Testimony. The edut is the pair of stone tablets put inside it (Exodus 25:16, 21), so the chest is named from its contents. It was acacia wood overlaid with gold, about three and three-quarter feet long by two and a quarter wide and high, carried on poles that were never taken out of their rings (Exodus 25:10-15).

Two different Hebrew words come into English as dry ground, and this account uses both: charavah at 3:17 and yabbashah at 4:22. Exodus used the same pair at the sea, charavah at 14:21 and yabbashah at 14:22. Verse 23 draws the comparison out loud, and the wording had already made it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Joshua directs twelve men to carry stones from the middle of the Jordan as a memorial; the priests remain in the riverbed until all Israel crosses, then the waters return to flood stage as the ark comes ashore.

stories.title: 🌊 Joshua 5
summaryBullets: Now when all the Amorite kings west of the Jordan and all the Canaanite kings along the coast heard how the LORD had dried up the waters of the Jordan before the Israelites until they had crossed over, their hearts melted and their spirits failed for fear of the Israelites. (5:1).
At that time the LORD said to Joshua, “Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel once again.” (5:2).
So Joshua made flint knives and circumcised the sons of Israel at Gibeath-haaraloth. (5:3).
Now this is why Joshua circumcised them: All those who came out of Egypt— all the men of war— had died on the journey in the wilderness after they had left Egypt. (5:4).
Though all who had come out were circumcised, none of those born in the wilderness on the journey from Egypt had been circumcised. (5:5).

For the Israelites had wandered in the wilderness forty years, until all the nation’s men of war who had come out of Egypt had died, since they did not obey the LORD. So the LORD vowed never to let them see the land He had sworn to their fathers to give us, a land flowing with milk and honey. (5:6).
And He raised up their sons in their place, and these were the ones Joshua circumcised. Until this time they were still uncircumcised, since they had not been circumcised along the way. (5:7).
And after all the nation had been circumcised, they stayed there in the camp until they were healed. (5:8).
Then the LORD said to Joshua, “Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you.” So that place has been called Gilgal to this day. (5:9).
On the evening of the fourteenth day of the month, while the Israelites were camped at Gilgal on the plains of Jericho, they kept the Passover. (5:10).
The day after the Passover, on that very day, they ate unleavened bread and roasted grain from the produce of the land. (5:11).
And the day after they had eaten from the produce of the land, the manna ceased. There was no more manna for the Israelites, so that year they began to eat the crops of the land of Canaan. (5:12).
Now when Joshua was near Jericho, he looked up and saw a man standing in front of him with a drawn sword in His hand. Joshua approached Him and asked, “Are You for us or for our enemies?” (5:13).
“Neither,” He replied. “I have now come as Commander of the LORD’s army.” Then Joshua fell facedown in reverence and asked Him, “What does my Lord have to say to His servant?” (5:14).
The Commander of the LORD’s army replied, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy.” And Joshua did so. (5:15).
crossRefs: Genesis 17:9-14: Every male among you shall be circumcised at eight days old, as the sign of the covenant.
Exodus 12:43-49: No uncircumcised person may eat the Passover, and a resident foreigner must be circumcised first.
Exodus 16:35: Israel ate manna forty years, until they came to the border of the land of Canaan.
Numbers 14:26-35: The generation that came out of Egypt will fall in the wilderness, and their children will go in.
Exodus 3:5: Take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.

translationNotes.note: Verse 9 explains the name: today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you. Gilgal echoes galal, to roll, and the place sits on the plain between the Jordan and Jericho, on the eastern edge of Jericho's fields (4:19). It becomes Israel's base camp for the whole campaign, and it is still a national gathering place in Samuel's day, where Saul is confirmed king (1 Samuel 11:14-15).

Verse 3 names the place, and the name says what happened there: the hill of the foreskins. A whole generation born on the march had never been circumcised, so before a single battle in Canaan the army takes the covenant sign and then lies up in enemy country until the men are healed (verse 8). Zipporah uses the same kind of blade in Exodus 4:25.

Verse 11 has Israel eat unleavened bread and roasted grain from the produce of the land the day after the Passover. Qali is fresh grain roasted over a fire, ordinary field food at harvest time; Boaz hands Ruth some at 2:14, and Jesse sends an ephah of it to his sons at 1 Samuel 17:17. Leviticus 23:14 forbids eating bread or parched grain from the new crop until the sheaf of firstfruits has been brought, so this is the first lawful food off the land, and the manna stops the next day.

Verse 2 has Joshua make knives of flint, at a time when Israel had bronze and knew of iron. Freshly struck flint takes an edge sharper than worked metal and can be knapped clean for each use, and it was the traditional implement for the rite; Zipporah uses one in Exodus 4:25. The choice is not backwardness but the old practice being resumed after forty years of neglect.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂר־צְבָא־יְהוָה (sar tseva YHWH), prince of the army of the LORD
translationNotes.note: Joshua asks a soldier's question, are you for us or for our enemies, and gets neither for an answer; the armies are the LORD's, and the question is which side Joshua is on. Verse 15 then gives the same command Moses was given at the burning bush, take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy (Exodus 3:5). Joshua falls on his face and is not told to get up.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Amorite and Canaanite kings hear of Israel's crossing and lose heart; Joshua circumcises the new generation at Gilgal, celebrates Passover, and encounters the commander of the LORD's army near Jericho. Israel eats Canaan's produce and the manna ceases.

headings.text: The Circumcision and Passover at Gilgal
The Commander of the Lord’s Army

stories.title: 🏰 Joshua 6
summaryBullets: Now Jericho was tightly shut up because of the Israelites. No one went out and no one came in. (6:1).
And the LORD said to Joshua, “Behold, I have delivered Jericho into your hand, along with its king and its mighty men of valor. (6:2).
March around the city with all the men of war, circling the city one time. Do this for six days. (6:3).
Have seven priests carry seven rams’ horns in front of the ark. Then on the seventh day, march around the city seven times, while the priests blow the horns. (6:4).

And when there is a long blast of the ram’s horn and you hear its sound, have all the people give a mighty shout. Then the wall of the city will collapse and all your people will charge straight into the city.” (6:5).
So Joshua son of Nun summoned the priests and said, “Take up the ark of the covenant and have seven priests carry seven rams’ horns in front of the ark of the LORD.” (6:6).
And he told the people, “Advance and march around the city, with the armed troops going ahead of the ark of the LORD.” (6:7).
After Joshua had spoken to the people, seven priests carrying seven rams’ horns before the LORD advanced and blew the horns, and the ark of the covenant of the LORD followed them. (6:8).
While the horns continued to sound, the armed troops marched ahead of the priests who blew the horns, and the rear guard followed the ark. (6:9).

But Joshua had commanded the people: “Do not give a battle cry or let your voice be heard; do not let one word come out of your mouth until the day I tell you to shout. Then you are to shout!” (6:10).
So he had the ark of the LORD carried around the city, circling it once. And the people returned to the camp and spent the night there. (6:11).
Joshua got up early the next morning, and the priests took the ark of the LORD. (6:12).

And the seven priests carrying seven rams’ horns kept marching ahead of the ark of the LORD and blowing the horns. The armed troops went in front of them and the rear guard followed the ark of the LORD, while the horns kept sounding. (6:13).
So on the second day they marched around the city once and returned to the camp. They did this for six days. (6:14).
Then on the seventh day, they got up at dawn and marched around the city seven times in the same manner. That was the only day they circled the city seven times. (6:15).
After the seventh time around, the priests blew the horns, and Joshua commanded the people, “Shout! For the LORD has given you the city! (6:16).
Now the city and everything in it must be devoted to the LORD for destruction. Only Rahab the prostitute and all those with her in her house will live, because she hid the spies we sent. (6:17).

But keep away from the things devoted to destruction, lest you yourself be set apart for destruction. If you take any of these, you will set apart the camp of Israel for destruction and bring disaster upon it. (6:18).
For all the silver and gold and all the articles of bronze and iron are holy to the LORD; they must go into His treasury.” (6:19).

So when the rams’ horns sounded, the people shouted. When they heard the blast of the horn, the people gave a great shout, and the wall collapsed. Then all the people charged straight into the city and captured it. (6:20).
With the edge of the sword they devoted to destruction everything in the city— man and woman, young and old, oxen, sheep, and donkeys. (6:21).
Meanwhile, Joshua told the two men who had spied out the land, “Go into the house of the prostitute and bring out the woman and all who are with her, just as you promised her.” (6:22).

So the young spies went in and brought out Rahab, her father and mother and brothers, and all who belonged to her. They brought out her whole family and settled them outside the camp of Israel. (6:23).
Then the Israelites burned up the city and everything in it. However, they put the silver and gold and articles of bronze and iron into the treasury of the LORD’s house. (6:24).

And Joshua spared Rahab the prostitute, with her father’s household and all who belonged to her, because she hid the men Joshua had sent to spy out Jericho. So she has lived among the Israelites to this day. (6:25).

At that time Joshua invoked this solemn oath: “Cursed before the LORD is the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho; at the cost of his firstborn he will lay its foundations; at the cost of his youngest he will set up its gates.” (6:26).
So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame spread throughout the land. (6:27).
crossRefs: Genesis 15:16: God tells Abram his descendants will not come back for four generations, 'for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete', which is the reason the land was left in place until now.

Deuteronomy 9:4-5: Israel is warned twice in two verses not to say the land is theirs for their own righteousness; the reasons given are the wickedness of these nations and the promise sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Deuteronomy 20:16-18: The command 6:21 carries out, with its reason attached in the same sentence: so that they cannot teach you to do all the detestable things they do for their gods.

Hebrews 11:30-31: The walls fall by faith after seven days, and the very next line has Rahab the prostitute not perishing with the disobedient because she welcomed the spies, which this chapter records.
1 Kings 16:34: Hiel of Bethel rebuilds Jericho and loses his firstborn and his youngest son, exactly as Joshua's oath in 6:26 said he would.

translationNotes.note: A walled oasis town in the Jordan valley about 850 feet below sea level, the lowest town on earth, fed year-round by a strong spring. It sits at the mouth of the pass that climbs west into the hill country, so it controls the road from the Jordan fords up to Jerusalem, Ai, and Bethel. Israel has to take it first because everything inland is behind it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שׁוֹפָר (shofar) - קֶרֶן הַיּוֹבֵל (qeren ha-yovel), horn of the ram
translationNotes.note: A shofar is a ram's horn, hollowed and heated and bent, with a hole cut at the tip. It has no reed and no valves and produces two or three notes, so it is not for tunes; it is a signal instrument. It announces the new moon and the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 25:9), calls out the militia (Judges 3:27), and sounded at Sinai (Exodus 19:16). Seven priests carry seven of them ahead of the ark here, once a day for six days and seven times on the seventh.

Cherem means put permanently out of ordinary use by handing it over to God, and verses 17 to 19 spell out both halves of it for Jericho. The living are destroyed; the silver, gold, bronze and iron are holy to the LORD and go into His treasury. Taking any of it does not merely rob the treasury, it makes the taker cherem as well, which is the sentence carried out in the next chapter.

translationNotes.term: The treasury of the LORD's house
translationNotes.note: Verses 19 and 24 keep the metal out of the fire and put it in the treasury. There was no temple yet, so the phrase means the store attached to the tabernacle and held by the Levites. Numbers 31:48-54 shows the same practice after the Midianite campaign, where the captured gold is weighed in and brought to the tent of meeting.

translationNotes.term: Cursed is the man who rebuilds Jericho
translationNotes.note: Verse 26 lays a public oath on whoever refounds the town: it will cost him his firstborn to lay the foundations and his youngest to set up the gates. People went on living at the site in between (Judges 3:13, 2 Samuel 10:5); the oath is against refortifying it. 1 Kings 16:34 records the outcome by name in Ahab's reign, when Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho and lost Abiram his firstborn and Segub his youngest.

stories.keyTakeaway: Joshua leads Israel around Jericho's walls once daily for six days with priests blowing trumpets, then seven times on the seventh day; when they shout on the final circuit, the wall collapses and they destroy the city, sparing only Rahab and her household.

stories.title: 🏰 Joshua 7
summaryBullets: The Israelites, however, acted unfaithfully regarding the things devoted to destruction. Achan son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of what was set apart. So the anger of the LORD burned against the Israelites. (7:1).
Meanwhile, Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, which is near Beth-aven to the east of Bethel, and told them, “Go up and spy out the land.” So the men went up and spied out Ai. (7:2).

On returning to Joshua, they reported, “There is no need to send all the people; two or three thousand men are enough to go up and attack Ai. Since the people of Ai are so few, you need not wear out all our people there.” (7:3).
So about three thousand men went up, but they fled before the men of Ai. (7:4).

And the men of Ai struck down about thirty-six of them, chasing them from the gate as far as the quarries and striking them down on the slopes. So the hearts of the people melted and became like water. (7:5).
Then Joshua tore his clothes and fell facedown before the ark of the LORD until evening, as did the elders of Israel; and they all sprinkled dust on their heads. (7:6).

“O, Lord GOD,” Joshua said, “why did You ever bring this people across the Jordan to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites to be destroyed? If only we had been content to stay on the other side of the Jordan! (7:7).
O Lord, what can I say, now that Israel has turned its back and run from its enemies? (7:8).
When the Canaanites and all who live in the land hear about this, they will surround us and wipe out our name from the earth. Then what will You do for Your great name?” (7:9).
But the LORD said to Joshua, “Stand up! Why have you fallen on your face? (7:10).

Israel has sinned; they have transgressed My covenant that I commanded them, and they have taken some of what was devoted to destruction. Indeed, they have stolen and lied, and they have put these things with their own possessions. (7:11).

This is why the Israelites cannot stand against their enemies. They will turn their backs and run from their enemies, because they themselves have been set apart for destruction. I will no longer be with you unless you remove from among you whatever is devoted to destruction. (7:12).

Get up and consecrate the people, saying, ‘Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, for this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: Among you, O Israel, there are things devoted to destruction. You cannot stand against your enemies until you remove them. (7:13).

In the morning you must present yourselves tribe by tribe. The tribe that the LORD selects shall come forward clan by clan, and the clan that the LORD selects shall come forward family by family, and the family that the LORD selects shall come forward man by man. (7:14).

The one who is caught with the things devoted to destruction must be burned, along with all that belongs to him, because he has transgressed the covenant of the LORD and committed an outrage in Israel.’” (7:15).
So Joshua arose early the next morning and had Israel come forward tribe by tribe, and the tribe of Judah was selected. (7:16).
He had the clans of Judah come forward, and the clan of the Zerahites was selected. He had the clan of the Zerahites come forward, and the family of Zabdi was selected. (7:17).
And he had the family of Zabdi come forward man by man, and Achan son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was selected. (7:18).
So Joshua said to Achan, “My son, give glory to the LORD, the God of Israel, and make a confession to Him. I urge you to tell me what you have done; do not hide it from me.” (7:19).
“It is true,” Achan replied, “I have sinned against the LORD, the God of Israel. This is what I did: (7:20).

When I saw among the spoils a beautiful cloak from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels, I coveted them and took them. They are hidden in the ground inside my tent, with the silver underneath.” (7:21).
So Joshua sent messengers who ran to the tent, and there it all was, hidden in his tent, with the silver underneath. (7:22).
They took the things from inside the tent, brought them to Joshua and all the Israelites, and spread them out before the LORD. (7:23).

Then Joshua, together with all Israel, took Achan son of Zerah, the silver, the cloak, the bar of gold, his sons and daughters, his oxen and donkeys and sheep, his tent, and everything else he owned, and brought them to the Valley of Achor. (7:24).

“Why have you brought this trouble upon us?” said Joshua. “Today the LORD will bring trouble upon you!” And all Israel stoned him to death. Then they stoned the others and burned their bodies. (7:25).
And they heaped over Achan a large pile of rocks that remains to this day. So the LORD turned from His burning anger. Therefore that place is called the Valley of Achor to this day. (7:26).
crossRefs: Leviticus 27:28-29: What is devoted to the LORD is most holy to Him and may not be sold or redeemed.
Deuteronomy 13:17: Let none of what is devoted to destruction stick to your hand, so that the LORD may turn from His burning anger.
Joshua 6:17-19: Jericho and everything in it are devoted, and the silver, gold, bronze, and iron go into the treasury of the LORD.
1 Chronicles 2:7: Achar, the troubler of Israel, who broke faith in the matter of the devoted thing.
Hosea 2:15: I will make the Valley of Achor a door of hope, and she shall answer there as in the days of her youth.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵמֶק עָכוֹר (Emeq Achor) - עָכַר (akar), to bring trouble on
translationNotes.note: The name comes out of the sentence Joshua passes in verse 25: you have brought trouble on us, so the LORD brings trouble on you today. The valley runs up from the Jordan plain toward the Judean hills and is a fixed point on Judah's northern boundary (15:7). Hosea 2:15 takes the same name the other way and calls it a door of hope.

Verse 21 itemises it: a fine robe from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels. That is about five pounds of silver and a pound and a quarter of gold, plus an imported garment from Mesopotamia. It was buried under his tent floor, which is where a household kept anything valuable, and it is dug out in front of the whole assembly in verse 23.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לָכַד (lakad), to be taken or caught
translationNotes.note: Verses 16 to 18 narrow the search in four steps: the tribes, then the clans of Judah, then the households of the Zerahites, then the men of one household. The method is the lot, the same procedure that chooses Saul in 1 Samuel 10:20-21. No witness accuses Achan and no one informs on him; the process produces him and he then confesses.

Verse 26 finishes by piling stones over the spot, and the writer adds that they are still there. The same marker goes up over the king of Ai (8:29) and over Absalom's body in the forest (2 Samuel 18:17). It is a public cairn, built to be seen from the road and to keep the account fastened to the place.

translationNotes.term: Tore his clothes and put dust on his head
translationNotes.note: Verse 6 has Joshua and the elders tear their clothes, lie face down before the ark until evening, and throw dust on their heads. Tearing the garment was the standard public sign of grief or horror, and it ruined a costly item, which was part of the meaning; dust or ashes on the head went with it (Job 2:12, 2 Samuel 13:19). This is a formal act performed in front of witnesses, not a loss of composure.

stories.keyTakeaway: Achan takes forbidden plunder from Jericho, causing Israel's defeat at Ai; Joshua identifies him through tribal casting, Achan confesses, and he and his household are destroyed in the Valley of Achor.

stories.title: 🏰 Joshua 8
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Joshua, “Do not be afraid or discouraged. Take the whole army with you, and go up and attack Ai. See, I have delivered into your hand the king of Ai, his people, his city, and his land. (8:1).
And you shall do to Ai and its king as you did to Jericho and its king, except that you may carry off their plunder and livestock for yourselves. Set up an ambush behind the city.” (8:2).
So Joshua and the whole army set out to attack Ai. Joshua chose 30,000 mighty men of valor and sent them out at night (8:3).
with these orders: “Pay attention. You are to lie in ambush behind the city, not too far from it. All of you must be ready. (8:4).
Then I and all the troops with me will advance on the city. When they come out against us as they did the first time, we will flee from them. (8:5).
They will pursue us until we have drawn them away from the city, for they will say, ‘The Israelites are running away from us as they did before.’ So as we flee from them, (8:6).
you are to rise from the ambush and seize the city, for the LORD your God will deliver it into your hand. (8:7).
And when you have taken the city, set it on fire. Do as the LORD has commanded! See, I have given you orders.” (8:8).
So Joshua sent them out, and they went to the place of ambush and lay in wait between Bethel and Ai, to the west of Ai. But Joshua spent that night among the people. (8:9).
Joshua got up early the next morning and mobilized his men, and he and the elders of Israel marched before them up to Ai. (8:10).
Then all the troops who were with him marched up and approached the city. They arrived in front of Ai and camped to the north of it, with the valley between them and the city. (8:11).
Now Joshua had taken about five thousand men and set up an ambush between Bethel and Ai, to the west of the city. (8:12).
So the forces were stationed with the main camp to the north of the city and the rear guard to the west of the city. And that night Joshua went into the valley. (8:13).

When the king of Ai saw the Israelites, he hurried out early in the morning with the men of the city to engage them in battle at an appointed place overlooking the Arabah. But he did not know that an ambush had been set up against him behind the city. (8:14).
Joshua and all Israel let themselves be beaten back before them, and they fled toward the wilderness. (8:15).
Then all the men of Ai were summoned to pursue them, and they followed Joshua and were drawn away from the city. (8:16).
Not a man was left in Ai or Bethel who did not go out after Israel, leaving the city wide open while they pursued Israel. (8:17).
Then the LORD said to Joshua, “Hold out your battle lance toward Ai, for into your hand I will deliver the city.” So Joshua held out his battle lance toward Ai, (8:18).
and as soon as he did so, the men in ambush rose quickly from their position. They rushed forward, entered the city, captured it, and immediately set it on fire. (8:19).

When the men of Ai turned and looked back, the smoke of the city was rising into the sky. They could not escape in any direction, and the troops who had fled to the wilderness now turned against their pursuers. (8:20).
When Joshua and all Israel saw that the men in ambush had captured the city and that smoke was rising from it, they turned around and struck down the men of Ai. (8:21).

Meanwhile, those in the ambush came out of the city against them, and the men of Ai were trapped between the Israelite forces on both sides. So Israel struck them down until no survivor or fugitive remained. (8:22).
But they took the king of Ai alive and brought him to Joshua. (8:23).

When Israel had finished killing all the men of Ai who had pursued them into the field and wilderness, and when every last one of them had fallen by the sword, all the Israelites returned to Ai and put it to the sword as well. (8:24).
A total of twelve thousand men and women fell that day— all the people of Ai. (8:25).
Joshua did not draw back the hand that held his battle lance until he had devoted to destruction all who lived in Ai. (8:26).
Israel took for themselves only the cattle and plunder of that city, as the LORD had commanded Joshua. (8:27).
So Joshua burned Ai and made it a permanent heap of ruins, a desolation to this day. (8:28).

He hung the king of Ai on a tree until evening, and at sunset Joshua commanded that they take down the body from the tree and throw it down at the entrance of the city gate. And over it they raised a large pile of rocks, which remains to this day. (8:29).
At that time Joshua built an altar on Mount Ebal to the LORD, the God of Israel, (8:30).

just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded the Israelites. He built it according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses: “an altar of uncut stones on which no iron tool has been used.” And on it they offered burnt offerings to the LORD, and they sacrificed peace offerings. (8:31).
And there in the presence of the Israelites, Joshua inscribed on the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he had written. (8:32).

All Israel, foreigners and citizens alike, with their elders, officers, and judges, stood on both sides of the ark of the covenant of the LORD facing the Levitical priests who carried it. Half of the people stood in front of Mount Gerizim and half of them in front of Mount Ebal, as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded earlier, to bless the people of Israel. (8:33).
Afterward, Joshua read aloud all the words of the law— the blessings and the curses— according to all that is written in the Book of the Law. (8:34).

There was not a word of all that Moses had commanded that Joshua failed to read before the whole assembly of Israel, including the women, the little ones, and the foreigners who lived among them. (8:35).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 27:1-8: Build an altar of uncut stones on Mount Ebal and write on the stones all the words of this law.
Deuteronomy 11:29: Set the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal.
Deuteronomy 31:10-13: Read this law before all Israel in their hearing, men, women, children, and the sojourner among you.
Exodus 20:25: If you make an altar of stone, do not build it of cut stones, for using a tool on it profanes it.
Deuteronomy 21:22-23: The body of a hanged man shall not remain overnight on the tree, but shall be buried the same day.

translationNotes.note: The town's name carries the definite article and means the ruin, which is what verse 28 makes it for good. It stands in the hills a mile or two east of Bethel, about twelve miles north of Jerusalem, watching the road that climbs from Jericho up onto the central ridge. Whoever holds Ai and Bethel holds the way inland, which is why Israel attacks it second.

Verses 18 and 26 have Joshua hold out a kidon toward Ai and not draw it back until the fighting is over. A kidon is a hand weapon, a javelin or short spear; it is the weapon slung between Goliath's shoulders at 1 Samuel 17:6. Held up, it is a visible signal to men lying in ambush on the far side of the town, and the posture matches Moses holding up his hand at Rephidim (Exodus 17:11-12).

translationNotes.term: Hung on a tree until evening
translationNotes.note: Verse 29 hangs the king of Ai on a tree and takes the body down at sunset. This is the public display of a corpse after execution, not the method of killing. Deuteronomy 21:22-23 requires the body to come down the same day, because a man hanged on a tree is under God's curse and the land must not be defiled; Paul quotes that verse in Galatians 3:13.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲבָנִים שְׁלֵמוֹת (avanim shelemot), whole stones
translationNotes.note: Verse 31 quotes the rule it is obeying: an altar of uncut stones on which no iron tool has been used. Exodus 20:25 gives it and says that swinging a tool on the stone profanes it, and Deuteronomy 27:5-6 repeats the rule for this exact altar on Ebal. What is built is a pile of field stones, not dressed masonry.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַר עֵיבָל (Har Eival) - הַר גְּרִזִים (Har Gerizim)
translationNotes.note: The two mountains stand on either side of the pass at Shechem, Ebal on the north at about 3,084 feet and Gerizim on the south at about 2,890. Moses assigned the curses to Ebal and the blessings to Gerizim (Deuteronomy 11:29, 27:11-13), and verses 33 to 35 have half the nation on each slope with the ark in the valley between. Adam Zertal excavated a large stone structure on Mount Ebal between 1982 and 1989 and identified it with this altar.

stories.keyTakeaway: Joshua sets an ambush to attack Ai, lures the king and his men away from the city, and destroys them completely; twelve thousand die and the city is burned. Joshua then builds an altar on Mount Ebal and reads the entire law of Moses to all Israel, including women, children, and foreigners.

stories.title: 🤝 Joshua 9
summaryBullets: Now when news of this reached all the kings west of the Jordan — those in the hill country, the foothills, and all along the coast of the Great Sea toward Lebanon (the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites)— (9:1).
they came together to wage war against Joshua and Israel. (9:2).
But the people of Gibeon, having heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai, (9:3).
acted deceptively and set out as envoys, carrying on their donkeys worn-out sacks and old wineskins, cracked and mended. (9:4).
They put worn, patched sandals on their feet and threadbare clothing on their bodies, and their whole supply of bread was dry and moldy. (9:5).
They went to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal and said to him and the men of Israel, “We have come from a distant land; please make a treaty with us.” (9:6).
But the men of Israel said to the Hivites, “Perhaps you dwell near us. How can we make a treaty with you?” (9:7).
“We are your servants,” they said to Joshua. Then Joshua asked them, “Who are you and where have you come from?” (9:8).
“Your servants have come from a very distant land,” they replied, “because of the fame of the LORD your God. For we have heard the reports about Him: all that He did in Egypt, (9:9).
and all that He did to the two kings of the Amorites beyond the Jordan— Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan, who reigned in Ashtaroth. (9:10).
So the elders and inhabitants of our land told us, ‘Take provisions for your journey; go to meet them and say to them: We are your servants. Please make a treaty with us.’ (9:11).
This bread of ours was warm when we packed it at home on the day we left to come to you. But look, it is now dry and moldy. (9:12).
These wineskins were new when we filled them, but look, they are cracked. And these clothes and sandals are worn out from our very long journey.” (9:13).
Then the men of Israel sampled their provisions but did not seek the counsel of the LORD. (9:14).
And Joshua made a treaty of peace with them to let them live, and the leaders of the congregation swore an oath to them. (9:15).
Three days after they had made the treaty with the Gibeonites, the Israelites learned that they were neighbors, living among them. (9:16).
So the Israelites set out and on the third day arrived at their cities — Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim. (9:17).

But the Israelites did not attack them, because the leaders of the congregation had sworn an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. And the whole congregation grumbled against the leaders. (9:18).
All the leaders answered, “We have sworn an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, and now we cannot touch them. (9:19).
This is how we will treat them: We will let them live, so that no wrath will fall on us because of the oath we swore to them.” (9:20).
They continued, “Let them live, but let them be woodcutters and water carriers for the whole congregation.” So the leaders kept their promise. (9:21).
Then Joshua summoned the Gibeonites and said, “Why did you deceive us by telling us you live far away from us, when in fact you live among us? (9:22).
Now therefore you are under a curse and will perpetually serve as woodcutters and water carriers for the house of my God.” (9:23).

The Gibeonites answered, “Your servants were told clearly that the LORD your God had commanded His servant Moses to give you all the land and wipe out all its inhabitants before you. So we greatly feared for our lives because of you, and that is why we have done this. (9:24).
Now we are in your hands. Do to us whatever seems good and right to you.” (9:25).
So Joshua did this and delivered them from the hands of the Israelites, and they did not kill the Gibeonites. (9:26).
On that day he made them woodcutters and water carriers, as they are to this day for the congregation of the LORD and for the altar at the place He would choose. (9:27).
crossRefs: Exodus 23:31-33: Make no covenant with them or with their gods, or they will make you sin against Me.
Deuteronomy 7:1-2: Make no covenant with them and show them no mercy when the LORD gives them over to you.
Deuteronomy 20:10-15: For cities very far off, offer terms of peace first, and their people shall become forced labour.
Numbers 30:2: If a man makes a vow to the LORD or swears an oath, he shall not break his word.
2 Samuel 21:1-9: Saul breaks this oath and puts Gibeonites to death, and the famine in David's day is the reckoning for it.

translationNotes.note: A large town about six miles northwest of Jerusalem on the central plateau, described in Joshua 10:2 as greater than Ai and a royal city. James Pritchard excavated it in the 1950s and uncovered a rock-cut pool about thirty-seven feet across and thirty-five deep with a spiral stair, which matches the pool of Gibeon in 2 Samuel 2:13, along with jar handles stamped with the town's name.

Verse 17 names them: Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth and Kiriath-jearim, all within a few miles of one another on the plateau north-west of Jerusalem. They are a small league acting together, which is why one delegation can bind all four. Kiriath-jearim is where the ark stood for twenty years after the Philistines sent it back (1 Samuel 7:1-2).

Verses 4, 12 and 13 build the disguise out of ordinary travelling kit. A wineskin was a whole goat hide, sewn and sealed with pitch; it stiffens and splits with age, which is why old skins burst when new wine works in them (Matthew 9:17). Cracked skins, dry crumbling bread and patched sandals are what a long road leaves behind, and they are the evidence Israel accepts instead of asking God.

translationNotes.term: They took some of their provisions
translationNotes.note: Verse 14 says the men of Israel sampled the Gibeonites' food and did not enquire of the LORD. Eating together is how an agreement was closed in that world: Isaac and Abimelech eat and drink and then swear (Genesis 26:30-31), Jacob and Laban eat bread on the heap of stones (Genesis 31:54), and the elders of Israel eat and drink before God on the mountain (Exodus 24:11). The shared meal is the signature, and it is why the oath in verse 15 cannot afterwards be undone.

translationNotes.term: Cutters of wood and drawers of water
translationNotes.note: The sentence in verses 21 to 27 is not slavery in a household but permanent conscripted service to the sanctuary. Both jobs were the heaviest daily labour a settlement needed: hauling firewood for the altar and carrying water up from a spring. Gibeon keeps its life and its town and loses its independence, and its men are still doing that work centuries later at the second temple (Nehemiah 3:7, Ezra 2:43-58).

stories.keyTakeaway: The Gibeonites deceive Joshua with worn provisions and false claims of distant origin to secure a peace treaty; after learning they are neighbors three days later, Joshua keeps the oath but makes them permanent servants as woodcutters and water carriers.

stories.title: 🤝 Joshua 10
summaryBullets: Now Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem heard that Joshua had captured Ai and devoted it to destruction — doing to Ai and its king as he had done to Jericho and its king — and that the people of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were living near them. (10:1).
So Adoni-zedek and his people were greatly alarmed, because Gibeon was a great city, like one of the royal cities; it was larger than Ai, and all its men were mighty. (10:2).
Therefore Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem sent word to Hoham king of Hebron, Piram king of Jarmuth, Japhia king of Lachish, and Debir king of Eglon, saying, (10:3).
“Come up and help me. We will attack Gibeon, because they have made peace with Joshua and the Israelites.” (10:4).

So the five kings of the Amorites— the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon— joined forces and advanced with all their armies. They camped before Gibeon and made war against it. (10:5).

Then the men of Gibeon sent word to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal: “Do not abandon your servants. Come quickly and save us! Help us, because all the kings of the Amorites from the hill country have joined forces against us.” (10:6).
So Joshua and his whole army, including all the mighty men of valor, came from Gilgal. (10:7).
The LORD said to Joshua, “Do not be afraid of them, for I have delivered them into your hand. Not one of them shall stand against you.” (10:8).
After marching all night from Gilgal, Joshua caught them by surprise. (10:9).

And the LORD threw them into confusion before Israel, who defeated them in a great slaughter at Gibeon, pursued them along the ascent to Beth-horon, and struck them down as far as Azekah and Makkedah. (10:10).

As they fled before Israel along the descent from Beth-horon to Azekah, the LORD cast down on them large hailstones from the sky, and more of them were killed by the hailstones than by the swords of the Israelites. (10:11).
On the day that the LORD gave the Amorites over to the Israelites, Joshua spoke to the LORD in the presence of Israel: “O sun, stand still over Gibeon, O moon, over the Valley of Aijalon.” (10:12).

So the sun stood still and the moon stopped until the nation took vengeance upon its enemies. Is this not written in the Book of Jashar? “So the sun stopped in the middle of the sky and delayed going down about a full day.” (10:13).
There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD listened to the voice of a man, because the LORD fought for Israel. (10:14).
Then Joshua returned with all Israel to the camp at Gilgal. (10:15).
Now the five kings had fled and hidden in the cave at Makkedah. (10:16).
And Joshua was informed: “The five kings have been found; they are hiding in the cave at Makkedah.” (10:17).
So Joshua said, “Roll large stones against the mouth of the cave, and post men there to guard them. (10:18).
But you, do not stop there. Pursue your enemies and attack them from behind. Do not let them reach their cities, for the LORD your God has delivered them into your hand.” (10:19).
So Joshua and the Israelites continued to inflict a terrible slaughter until they had finished them off, and the remaining survivors retreated to the fortified cities. (10:20).
The whole army returned safely to Joshua in the camp at Makkedah, and no one dared to utter a word against the Israelites. (10:21).
Then Joshua said, “Open the mouth of the cave and bring those five kings out to me.” (10:22).
So they brought the five kings out of the cave — the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon. (10:23).

When they had brought the kings to Joshua, he summoned all the men of Israel and said to the army commanders who had accompanied him, “Come here and put your feet on the necks of these kings.” So the commanders came forward and put their feet on their necks. (10:24).
“Do not be afraid or discouraged,” Joshua said. “Be strong and courageous, for the LORD will do this to all the enemies you fight.” (10:25).
After this, Joshua struck down and killed the kings, and he hung their bodies on five trees and left them there until evening. (10:26).

At sunset Joshua ordered that they be taken down from the trees and thrown into the cave in which they had hidden. Then large stones were placed against the mouth of the cave, and the stones are there to this day. (10:27).

On that day Joshua captured Makkedah and put it to the sword, along with its king. He devoted to destruction everyone in the city, leaving no survivors. So he did to the king of Makkedah as he had done to the king of Jericho. (10:28).
Then Joshua and all Israel with him moved on from Makkedah to Libnah and fought against Libnah. (10:29).

And the LORD also delivered that city and its king into the hand of Israel, and Joshua put all the people to the sword, leaving no survivors. And he did to the king of Libnah as he had done to the king of Jericho. (10:30).
And Joshua and all Israel with him moved on from Libnah to Lachish. They laid siege to it and fought against it. (10:31).
And the LORD delivered Lachish into the hand of Israel, and Joshua captured it on the second day. He put all the people to the sword, just as he had done to Libnah. (10:32).
At that time Horam king of Gezer went to help Lachish, but Joshua struck him down along with his people, leaving no survivors. (10:33).
So Joshua moved on from Lachish to Eglon, and all Israel with him. They laid siege to it and fought against it. (10:34).
That day they captured Eglon and put it to the sword, and Joshua devoted to destruction everyone in the city, just as he had done to Lachish. (10:35).
Then Joshua and all Israel with him went up from Eglon to Hebron and fought against it. (10:36).

They captured it and put to the sword its king, all its villages, and all the people. Joshua left no survivors, just as he had done at Eglon; he devoted to destruction Hebron and everyone in it. (10:37).
Finally Joshua and all Israel with him turned toward Debir and fought against it. (10:38).

And they captured Debir, its king, and all its villages. They put them to the sword and devoted to destruction everyone in the city, leaving no survivors. Joshua did to Debir and its king as he had done to Hebron and as he had done to Libnah and its king. (10:39).

So Joshua conquered the whole region— the hill country, the Negev, the foothills, and the slopes, together with all their kings— leaving no survivors. He devoted to destruction everything that breathed, just as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded. (10:40).
Joshua conquered the area from Kadesh-barnea to Gaza, and the whole region of Goshen as far as Gibeon. (10:41).
And because the LORD, the God of Israel, fought for Israel, Joshua captured all these kings and their land in one campaign. (10:42).
Then Joshua returned with all Israel to the camp at Gilgal. (10:43).
crossRefs: Joshua 9:15-20: The oath sworn to Gibeon, which is why Israel marches all night to defend a town it was tricked by.
Exodus 14:24-25: The LORD looks down on the Egyptian army from the pillar of fire and cloud and throws it into a panic.
Habakkuk 3:11: The sun and moon stood still in their place at the light of Your arrows as they sped.
2 Samuel 1:18: David's lament over Saul is written in the Book of Jashar, the same record cited in verse 13.
Deuteronomy 21:22-23: A hanged body must not remain on the tree overnight, but be buried the same day, as verse 27 does.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲדֹנִי־צֶדֶק (Adoni-tsedeq), my lord is righteousness
translationNotes.note: Verse 3 lists the coalition by city: Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon. Those are the towns of the southern hill country and the foothills below it, and between them they hold every road into Judah from the coast. The king of Jerusalem's name is built the same way as Melchizedek, king of Salem, in Genesis 14:18.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַבְנֵי בָרָד (avnei barad), stones of hail
translationNotes.note: Verse 11 counts the dead separately: more of them were killed by the hailstones than Israel killed with the sword, and the hail falls on them as they run down the descent from Beth-horon. Storms driving in off the Mediterranean do produce hail in that country, though rarely on this scale. The text names who sent it and leaves the tally standing.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֵפֶר הַיָּשָׁר (sefer ha-yashar), the book of the upright
translationNotes.note: Verse 13 quotes the sun and moon lines out of a book called Jashar, which means the first readers already had a collection of Israelite war poetry they could check it against. The same book is cited once more, for David's lament over Saul and Jonathan, at 2 Samuel 1:18. It has not survived; Scripture is citing a source the way any writer cites one.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֶׁמֶשׁ בְּגִבְעוֹן דּוֹם (shemesh be-Givon dom)
translationNotes.note: The verb dom means be still, or be silent. Joshua addresses the sun over Gibeon and the moon over the Valley of Aijalon, the two of them in the sky together, and verse 13 reports that the sun stopped in the middle of the sky and did not hurry to set for about a whole day. Verse 14 states plainly that there has been no day like it before or since, so the account presents it as unrepeated rather than as anything ordinary.

translationNotes.term: Feet on the necks of the kings
translationNotes.note: Verse 24 has the commanders put their feet on the necks of the five captured kings. It is a formal act of subjection with a fixed meaning, not an insult improvised on the day; Egyptian and Assyrian palace reliefs show conquered men in the same posture, and Psalm 110:1 turns it into a figure when it makes enemies a footstool. The kings are then executed, hung until evening, and sealed in the cave they had hidden in.

Verses 10 and 11 chase the five kings down the descent of Beth-horon, the main road from the central ridge down to the Aijalon valley and the coastal plain. Upper and Lower Beth-horon guard the two ends of a steep, narrow climb, which is why armies fought for it from Joshua's day to the Maccabees. An army caught strung out on that descent has no room to turn and fight.

stories.keyTakeaway: Five Amorite kings unite against Gibeon; Joshua marches from Gilgal, routs them with divine help including hail and extended daylight, then executes the five kings and systematically destroys Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, and Debir.
