stories.title: 🤝 Joshua 11
summaryBullets: Now when Jabin king of Hazor heard about these things, he sent word to Jobab king of Madon; to the kings of Shimron and Achshaph; (11:1).
to the kings of the north in the mountains, in the Arabah south of Chinnereth, in the foothills, and in Naphoth-dor to the west; (11:2).
to the Canaanites in the east and west; to the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, and Jebusites in the hill country; and to the Hivites at the foot of Hermon in the land of Mizpah. (11:3).
So these kings came out with all their armies, a multitude as numerous as the sand on the seashore, along with a great number of horses and chariots. (11:4).
All these kings joined forces and encamped at the waters of Merom to fight against Israel. (11:5).

Then the LORD said to Joshua, “Do not be afraid of them, for by this time tomorrow I will deliver all of them slain before Israel. You are to hamstring their horses and burn up their chariots.” (11:6).
So by the waters of Merom, Joshua and his whole army came upon them suddenly and attacked them, (11:7).

and the LORD delivered them into the hand of Israel, who struck them down and pursued them all the way to Greater Sidon and Misrephoth-maim, and eastward as far as the Valley of Mizpeh. They struck them down, leaving no survivors. (11:8).
Joshua treated them as the LORD had told him; he hamstrung their horses and burned up their chariots. (11:9).
At that time Joshua turned back and captured Hazor and put its king to the sword, because Hazor was formerly the head of all these kingdoms. (11:10).
The Israelites put everyone in Hazor to the sword, devoting them to destruction. Nothing that breathed remained, and Joshua burned down Hazor itself. (11:11).
Joshua captured all these kings and their cities and put them to the sword. He devoted them to destruction, as Moses the LORD’s servant had commanded. (11:12).
Yet Israel did not burn any of the cities built on their mounds, except Hazor, which Joshua burned. (11:13).

The Israelites took for themselves all the plunder and livestock of these cities, but they put all the people to the sword until they had completely destroyed them, not sparing anyone who breathed. (11:14).
As the LORD had commanded His servant Moses, so Moses commanded Joshua. That is what Joshua did, leaving nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses. (11:15).
So Joshua took this entire region: the hill country, all the Negev, all the land of Goshen, the western foothills, the Arabah, and the mountains of Israel and their foothills, (11:16).
from Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir, as far as Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon at the foot of Mount Hermon. He captured all their kings and struck them down, putting them to death. (11:17).
Joshua waged war against all these kings for a long period of time. (11:18).
No city made peace with the Israelites except the Hivites living in Gibeon; all others were taken in battle. (11:19).

For it was of the LORD to harden their hearts to engage Israel in battle, so that they would be set apart for destruction and would receive no mercy, being annihilated as the LORD had commanded Moses. (11:20).

At that time Joshua proceeded to eliminate the Anakim from the hill country of Hebron, Debir, and Anab, and from all the hill country of Judah and of Israel. Joshua devoted them to destruction, along with their cities. (11:21).
No Anakim were left in the land of the Israelites; only in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod did any survive. (11:22).

So Joshua took the entire land, in keeping with all that the LORD had spoken to Moses. And Joshua gave it as an inheritance to Israel according to the allotments to their tribes. Then the land had rest from war. (11:23).
crossRefs: Genesis 15:16: The land is left alone for four generations 'for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete', the stated reason this campaign happens when it does and not earlier.
Deuteronomy 9:4-5: Not for your righteousness, Moses says, but for the wickedness of these nations and to keep the promise sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Deuteronomy 20:16-18: The command 11:12 says Joshua was carrying out, given there with the reason attached: so that they cannot teach you to do all the detestable things they do for their gods.
Deuteronomy 7:1-2: The seven nations are named and the order to devote them to destruction is given, which is what 11:15 says Joshua left nothing undone of.
Judges 4:1-3: A later Jabin of Hazor with nine hundred iron chariots oppresses Israel for twenty years, in the city 11:10-11 burned to the ground.

translationNotes.note: Verses 5 and 7 put the whole northern coalition in one camp at the waters of Merom, in the uplands of Galilee north-west of the Sea of Galilee. It is one of the few places in that broken country with room to assemble horses and chariots in numbers. Verse 7 says Joshua and his whole army came on them there suddenly.

Verse 10 calls Hazor the head of all those kingdoms, and the site bears it out: Tel Hazor in upper Galilee is the largest ancient mound in Israel, roughly two hundred acres with an upper citadel and a walled lower city, sitting on the trade road from Egypt to Mesopotamia. Yigael Yadin excavated it from 1955 to 1958 and found a violent destruction layer with burned mudbrick and smashed statuary. Verse 11 says Joshua burned Hazor with fire, and only Hazor.

Verses 6 and 9 have Israel cripple the captured horses by cutting the tendon at the back of the hock and burn the chariots rather than keep them. Chariots were the dominant weapon of the coalition and the one thing Israel could have taken over. The order removes the technology from the field instead, which is the same policy Deuteronomy 17:16 sets for Israel's future kings.

Verses 11 to 15 show that the ban was not one blanket rule applied the same way everywhere. Hazor alone is burned. The other towns still standing on their mounds are left standing (verse 13), and verse 14 says Israel took the livestock and the goods of those cities as plunder for themselves. The account insists Joshua left nothing undone of what Moses commanded, and what Moses commanded was this specific about what burns and what is kept.

Verses 21 and 22 clear the Anakim out of Hebron, Debir and Anab in the hill country. These are the tall clans the twelve reported on at Numbers 13:28 and 33, and Deuteronomy 9:2 quotes the proverb about them: who can stand before the sons of Anak? Verse 22 records where the survivors went, to Gaza, Gath and Ashdod, which is the town Goliath of Gath comes from in 1 Samuel 17.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jabin of Hazor rallies multiple northern kings and their armies against Israel; Joshua defeats them at the Waters of Merom, then destroys Hazor and captures all the royal cities, eliminating their kings and populations as the Lord commanded. Joshua conquers the entire region from Mount Halak to Baal Gad, destroys the Anakites, and distributes the land to Israel's tribes.

stories.title: 🤝 Joshua 12
summaryBullets: Now these are the kings of the land whom the Israelites struck down and whose lands they took beyond the Jordan to the east, from the Arnon Valley to Mount Hermon, including all the Arabah eastward: (12:1).

Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon. He ruled from Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley, along the middle of the valley, up to the Jabbok River (the border of the Ammonites), that is, half of Gilead, (12:2).
as well as the Arabah east of the Sea of Chinnereth to the Sea of the Arabah (the Salt Sea), eastward through Beth-jeshimoth, and southward below the slopes of Pisgah. (12:3).
And Og king of Bashan, one of the remnant of the Rephaim, who lived in Ashtaroth and Edrei. (12:4).
He ruled over Mount Hermon, Salecah, all of Bashan up to the border of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and half of Gilead to the border of Sihon king of Heshbon. (12:5).
Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the Israelites had struck them down and given their land as an inheritance to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. (12:6).

And these are the kings of the land that Joshua and the Israelites conquered beyond the Jordan to the west, from Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon to Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir (according to the allotments to the tribes of Israel, Joshua gave them as an inheritance (12:7).
the hill country, the foothills, the Arabah, the slopes, the wilderness, and the Negev — the lands of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites): (12:8).
the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is near Bethel, one; (12:9).
the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one; (12:10).
the king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one; (12:11).
the king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one; (12:12).
the king of Debir, one; the king of Geder, one; (12:13).
the king of Hormah, one; the king of Arad, one; (12:14).
the king of Libnah, one; the king of Adullam, one; (12:15).
the king of Makkedah, one; the king of Bethel, one; (12:16).
the king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one; (12:17).
the king of Aphek, one; the king of Lasharon, one; (12:18).
the king of Madon, one; the king of Hazor, one; (12:19).
the king of Shimron-meron, one; the king of Achshaph, one; (12:20).
the king of Taanach, one; the king of Megiddo, one; (12:21).
the king of Kedesh, one; the king of Jokneam in Carmel, one; (12:22).
the king of Dor in Naphath-dor, one; the king of Goiim in Gilgal, one; (12:23).
and the king of Tirzah, one. So there were thirty-one kings in all. (12:24).
crossRefs: Numbers 21:21-35: Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan refuse Israel passage, and their land is taken.
Deuteronomy 2:24-3:11: The same two kings, with the note that Og's iron bedstead was nine cubits long.
Deuteronomy 3:8-17: The territory taken from the two Amorite kings, from the Arnon gorge to Mount Hermon.
Joshua 13:1-7: Much land still remains to be possessed, set out immediately after this record of victories.
Psalm 135:10-12: He struck down many nations and killed mighty kings, Sihon and Og, and gave their land as a heritage.

translationNotes.note: Verse 24 totals the list at thirty-one. A Canaanite king ruled one walled town with its fields and villages, not a country; the land was a patchwork of city-states, each with its own ruler and its own quarrels. Nearly four hundred clay tablets found at Tell el-Amarna in Egypt in 1887, letters written to Pharaoh in the fourteenth century BC, come from rulers of exactly this kind at Jerusalem, Gezer, Lachish, Megiddo and Shechem.

Verse 1 fixes the eastern conquests between two landmarks. The Arnon is a gorge more than a thousand feet deep running west into the Dead Sea, the northern boundary of Moab, and an army has to climb down into it and out again to cross. Hermon at the far north rises to 9,232 feet, holds snow most of the year, and its meltwater feeds the springs that become the Jordan.

Verse 4 calls Og one of the remnant of the Rephaim and puts his two capitals at Ashtaroth and Edrei in Bashan, the high grain plateau east of the Sea of Galilee. Rephaim is the term for the tall peoples who held the land before Israel; Deuteronomy 2:10-11 and 20-21 say the Moabites called them Emim and the Ammonites Zamzummim. Deuteronomy 3:11 supplies the one measurement given anywhere: Og's iron bedstead was nine cubits by four, about thirteen and a half feet by six.

translationNotes.term: The Sea of Chinnereth and the Salt Sea
translationNotes.note: Two lakes on the same river, and the text uses both to mark boundaries. Chinnereth is the fresh-water lake later called the Sea of Galilee, about thirteen miles long and eight wide, its surface some 700 feet below sea level. The Salt Sea is the Dead Sea at the bottom of the same rift, more than 1,300 feet below sea level, roughly ten times as salty as the ocean, with no outlet and no fish in it.

Verse 21 lists two towns about five miles apart that guard the passes through the Carmel ridge, where the main road from Egypt to Damascus squeezes out of the hills into the Jezreel plain. Whoever holds Megiddo holds that road, which is why armies fought over it for three thousand years; Pharaoh Thutmose III took it about 1457 BC and had the account carved on the temple walls at Karnak. Revelation 16:16 names the gathering place Armageddon, which is the Greek form of Har Megiddo, the hill of Megiddo.

stories.keyTakeaway: Joshua lists the kings defeated east of the Jordan under Moses - Sihon and Og - and then catalogs thirty-one kings defeated west of the Jordan under his own command, with their territories distributed to the Israelite tribes.

stories.title: 🗺️ Joshua 13
summaryBullets: Now Joshua was old and well along in years, and the LORD said to him, “You are old and well along in years, but very much of the land remains to be possessed. (13:1).
This is the land that remains: All the territory of the Philistines and the Geshurites, (13:2).

from the Shihor east of Egypt to the territory of Ekron on the north (considered to be Canaanite territory)— that of the five Philistine rulers of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron, as well as that of the Avvites; (13:3).
to the south, all the land of the Canaanites, from Mearah of the Sidonians to Aphek, as far as the border of the Amorites; (13:4).
the land of the Gebalites; and all Lebanon to the east, from Baal-gad below Mount Hermon to Lebo-hamath. (13:5).

All the inhabitants of the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim — all the Sidonians — I Myself will drive out before the Israelites. Be sure to divide it by lot as an inheritance to Israel, as I have commanded you. (13:6).
Now therefore divide this land as an inheritance to the nine tribes and the half-tribe of Manasseh.” (13:7).

The other half of Manasseh, along with the Reubenites and Gadites, had received the inheritance Moses had given them beyond the Jordan to the east, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had assigned to them: (13:8).
The area from Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley, along with the city in the middle of the valley, the whole plateau of Medeba as far as Dibon, (13:9).
and all the cities of Sihon king of the Amorites who reigned in Heshbon, as far as the border of the Ammonites; (13:10).
also Gilead and the territory of the Geshurites and Maacathites, all of Mount Hermon, and all Bashan as far as Salecah— (13:11).
the whole kingdom of Og in Bashan, who had reigned in Ashtaroth and Edrei and had remained as a remnant of the Rephaim. Moses had struck them down and dispossessed them, (13:12).
but the Israelites did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites. So Geshur and Maacath dwell among the Israelites to this day. (13:13).
To the tribe of Levi, however, Moses had given no inheritance. The food offerings to the LORD, the God of Israel, are their inheritance, just as He had promised them. (13:14).
This is what Moses had given to the clans of the tribe of Reuben: (13:15).
The territory from Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley, along with the city in the middle of the valley, to the whole plateau beyond Medeba, (13:16).
to Heshbon and all its cities on the plateau, including Dibon, Bamoth-baal, Beth-baal-meon, (13:17).
Jahaz, Kedemoth, Mephaath, (13:18).
Kiriathaim, Sibmah, Zereth-shahar on the hill in the valley, (13:19).
Beth-peor, the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth-jeshimoth— (13:20).

all the cities of the plateau and all the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon until Moses killed him and the chiefs of Midian (Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba), the princes of Sihon who lived in the land. (13:21).
The Israelites also killed the diviner Balaam son of Beor along with the others they put to the sword. (13:22).
And the border of the Reubenites was the bank of the Jordan. This was the inheritance of the clans of the Reubenites, including the cities and villages. (13:23).
This is what Moses had given to the clans of the tribe of Gad: (13:24).
The territory of Jazer, all the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the Ammonites as far as Aroer, near Rabbah; (13:25).
the territory from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh and Betonim, and from Mahanaim to the border of Debir; (13:26).

and in the valley, Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth, and Zaphon, with the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon (the territory on the east side of the Jordan up to the edge of the Sea of Chinnereth). (13:27).
This was the inheritance of the clans of the Gadites, including the cities and villages. (13:28).
This is what Moses had given to the clans of the half-tribe of Manasseh, that is, to half the tribe of the descendants of Manasseh: (13:29).
The territory from Mahanaim through all Bashan— all the kingdom of Og king of Bashan, including all the towns of Jair that are in Bashan, sixty cities; (13:30).

half of Gilead; and Ashtaroth and Edrei, the royal cities of Og in Bashan. All this was for the clans of the descendants of Machir son of Manasseh, that is, half of the descendants of Machir. (13:31).
These were the portions Moses had given them on the plains of Moab beyond the Jordan, east of Jericho. (13:32).
To the tribe of Levi, however, Moses had given no inheritance. The LORD, the God of Israel, is their inheritance, just as He had promised them. (13:33).
crossRefs: Numbers 32:1-42: Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh ask Moses for the grazing land east of the Jordan.
Deuteronomy 3:12-17: Moses assigns the land from Aroer by the Arnon to the Jordan valley and the Sea of the Arabah.
Numbers 18:20-24: Aaron is told he shall have no inheritance in their land, for the LORD is his portion.
Numbers 31:8: Balaam son of Beor is killed with the sword among the kings of Midian, as verse 22 recalls.
Judges 3:1-4: The nations left in the land, and the reason they were left there.

translationNotes.note: A nachalah is a family holding passed down the generations, not a purchase and not a wage. The land is held from the LORD, who says in Leviticus 25:23 that the land is His and Israel are tenants on it, and it is not supposed to leave the family. Verses 14 and 33 make Levi the exception twice: in verse 14 the food offerings are Levi's inheritance, and in verse 33 the LORD Himself is. The tribe that serves at the altar owns no ground.

Verse 3 lists the Philistine cities as Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron, strung along and behind the coastal plain from the edge of Egypt up to the Judean foothills. Scripture uses a special word for their rulers, seren, and uses it for no one else, never for an Israelite or Canaanite king. The five acted as a council and decided together, which is why all five make one ruling about the captured ark at 1 Samuel 5:8 and 6:16.

Verses 9, 16 and 17 keep calling Reuben's country the mishor, the flat tableland running north from the Arnon: high, open, and good for grain and grazing. That is exactly why Reuben and Gad asked Moses for it rather than crossing the river (Numbers 32:1-5). Moab took much of it back later, and the inscription of King Mesha of Moab, cut about 840 BC and found at Dhiban in Jordan in 1868, names Medeba, Ataroth, Nebo and Jahaz among the towns he says he retook from Israel.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּמוֹת בַּעַל (Bamoth Baal), high places of Baal - בַּעַל פְּעוֹר (Baal Peor)
translationNotes.note: Verses 17 and 20 hand Reuben towns whose names are the names of Canaanite worship sites. A bamah is a high place, an open-air platform with an altar on a hill or ridge, so Bamoth-baal means the high places of Baal. Beth-peor is the house of Peor, and Baal of Peor is the god Israel joined in worshipping in this very country, at a cost of twenty-four thousand dead (Numbers 25:1-9). Moses is buried in the valley opposite it (Deuteronomy 34:6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַקּוֹסֵם (ha-qosem), the one who practises divination
translationNotes.note: Verse 22 identifies Balaam son of Beor by his trade: he was a professional diviner, a man hired to read omens and pronounce blessings and curses (Numbers 22:7). A plaster inscription found at Tell Deir Alla in Jordan in 1967 opens with the sayings of Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods, which puts his name in a text from the region outside Scripture.

stories.keyTakeaway: God tells the aged Joshua that much land remains unconquered and details the territories still to be taken; the chapter then records the inheritance Moses had already given to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh east of the Jordan, and notes that Levi received no land inheritance since the LORD's offerings are theirs.

headings.text: The Inheritance East of the Jordan

stories.title: 🗺️ Joshua 14
summaryBullets: Now these are the portions that the Israelites inherited in the land of Canaan, as distributed by Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the heads of the families of the tribes of Israel. (14:1).
Their inheritance was assigned by lot for the nine and a half tribes, as the LORD had commanded through Moses. (14:2).
For Moses had given the inheritance east of the Jordan to the other two and a half tribes. But he granted no inheritance among them to the Levites. (14:3).

The descendants of Joseph became two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. And no portion of the land was given to the Levites, except for cities in which to live, along with pasturelands for their flocks and herds. (14:4).
So the Israelites did as the LORD had commanded Moses, and they divided the land. (14:5).

Then the sons of Judah approached Joshua at Gilgal, and Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite said to him, “You know what the LORD said to Moses the man of God at Kadesh-barnea about you and me. (14:6).
I was forty years old when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land, and I brought back to him an honest report. (14:7).
Although my brothers who went with me made the hearts of the people melt with fear, I remained loyal to the LORD my God. (14:8).
On that day Moses swore to me, saying, ‘Surely the land on which you have set foot will be an inheritance to you and your children forever, because you have wholly followed the LORD my God.’ (14:9).

Now behold, as the LORD promised, He has kept me alive these forty-five years since He spoke this word to Moses, while Israel wandered in the wilderness. So here I am today, eighty-five years old, (14:10).
still as strong today as I was the day Moses sent me out. As my strength was then, so it is now for war, for going out, and for coming in. (14:11).

Now therefore give me this hill country that the LORD promised me on that day, for you yourself heard then that the Anakim were there, with great and fortified cities. Perhaps with the LORD’s help I will drive them out, as the LORD has spoken.” (14:12).
Then Joshua blessed Caleb son of Jephunneh and gave him Hebron as his inheritance. (14:13).
Therefore Hebron belongs to Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite as an inheritance to this day, because he wholly followed the LORD, the God of Israel. (14:14).
(Hebron used to be called Kiriath-arba, after Arba, the greatest man among the Anakim.) Then the land had rest from war. (14:15).
crossRefs: Numbers 13:30: Caleb quiets the people before Moses and says, let us go up at once and take it, for we are well able.
Numbers 14:20-24: Caleb, because he had a different spirit and followed fully, will be brought into the land.
Deuteronomy 1:34-36: None of this generation shall see the land except Caleb, who shall have the ground he walked on.
Joshua 15:13-14: Caleb drives the three sons of Anak out of Hebron and takes the town for himself.
Numbers 34:16-29: Eleazar, Joshua, and one leader from each tribe are appointed to divide the land as an inheritance.

translationNotes.note: Verse 1 names three parties who divide the land together: Eleazar the priest, Joshua the commander, and the heads of the tribal families. Eleazar was Aaron's third son and took his father's office when Aaron died on Mount Hor (Numbers 20:25-28). The priest is present because the allotment is settled by lot before the LORD (verse 2), not by bargaining between tribes.

Verses 6 and 7 keep pointing back to Kadesh-barnea, an oasis on the edge of the Wilderness of Zin about fifty miles south-west of Beersheba. Israel camped there, the twelve were sent from there to spy out the land and brought their report back there (Numbers 13:26), and there the generation that refused to go up was sentenced to die in the wilderness (Numbers 14:20-35). Every claim Caleb makes in this chapter dates from that place.

translationNotes.term: Forty-five years, and about seven years of fighting
translationNotes.note: Verses 7 and 10 give hard numbers: Caleb was forty at Kadesh-barnea and is eighty-five now, so forty-five years have gone by. Deuteronomy 2:14 accounts for thirty-eight of them, between Kadesh-barnea and the crossing of the Zered. That leaves roughly seven years between the crossing of the Jordan and this conversation, and it is the only measure Scripture gives for how long the campaigns of chapters 6 to 12 took.

Verse 15 gives the town's older name and says Arba was the greatest man among the Anakim. Hebron stands about 3,000 feet up in the southern hill country, some nineteen miles south of Jerusalem, the highest town in Judah. Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah there for four hundred shekels of silver as a burial plot (Genesis 23:16-20), and David reigned there seven years before taking Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:5).

Verses 6 and 14 call Caleb the Kenizzite. Kenaz appears in Esau's line as a chief of Edom (Genesis 36:11,15), so Caleb's clan came into Israel from outside and was reckoned within the tribe of Judah (Numbers 13:6). The man who gets the first and best portion of the land is a man whose family joined Israel rather than descending from Jacob directly.

stories.keyTakeaway: Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal leaders allot the land of Canaan to the nine-and-a-half tribes by lot, with the Levites receiving towns instead of land; Caleb approaches Joshua and claims Hebron as his inheritance, reminding him of God's promise made forty-five years earlier, and Joshua grants it to him.

headings.text: Land Division West of the Jordan

stories.title: 🗺️ Joshua 15
summaryBullets: Now the allotment for the clans of the tribe of Judah extended to the border of Edom, to the Wilderness of Zin at the extreme southern boundary: (15:1).
Their southern border started at the bay on the southern tip of the Salt Sea, (15:2).
proceeded south of the Ascent of Akrabbim, continued on to Zin, went over to the south of Kadesh-barnea, ran past Hezron up to Addar, and curved toward Karka. (15:3).
It proceeded to Azmon, joined the Brook of Egypt, and ended at the Sea. This was their southern border. (15:4).
The eastern border was the Salt Sea as far as the mouth of the Jordan. The northern border started from the bay of the sea at the mouth of the Jordan, (15:5).
went up to Beth-hoglah, proceeded north of Beth-arabah, and went up to the Stone of Bohan son of Reuben. (15:6).

Then the border went up to Debir from the Valley of Achor, turning north to Gilgal, which faces the Ascent of Adummim south of the ravine. It continued along the waters of En-shemesh and came out at En-rogel. (15:7).

From there the border went up the Valley of Ben-hinnom along the southern slope of the Jebusites (that is, Jerusalem) and ascended to the top of the hill that faces the Valley of Hinnom on the west, at the northern end of the Valley of Rephaim. (15:8).
From the hilltop the border curved to the spring of the Waters of Nephtoah, proceeded to the cities of Mount Ephron, and then bent around toward Baalah (that is, Kiriath-jearim). (15:9).
The border curled westward from Baalah to Mount Seir, ran along the northern slope of Mount Jearim (that is, Chesalon), went down to Beth-shemesh, and crossed to Timnah. (15:10).
Then it went out to the northern slope of Ekron, curved toward Shikkeron, proceeded to Mount Baalah, went on to Jabneel, and ended at the Sea. (15:11).
And the western border was the coastline of the Great Sea. These are the boundaries around the clans of the descendants of Judah. (15:12).
According to the LORD’s command to him, Joshua gave Caleb son of Jephunneh a portion among the sons of Judah — Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron. (Arba was the forefather of Anak.) (15:13).
And Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak — the descendants of Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak. (15:14).
From there he marched against the inhabitants of Debir (formerly known as Kiriath-sepher). (15:15).
And Caleb said, “To the man who strikes down Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage.” (15:16).
So Othniel son of Caleb’s brother Kenaz captured the city, and Caleb gave his daughter Acsah to him in marriage. (15:17).
One day Acsah came to Othniel and urged him to ask her father for a field. When she got off her donkey, Caleb asked her, “What do you desire?” (15:18).
“Give me a blessing,” she answered. “Since you have given me land in the Negev, give me springs of water as well.” So Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs. (15:19).
This is the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Judah. (15:20).
These were the southernmost cities of the tribe of Judah in the Negev toward the border of Edom: Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur, (15:21).
Kinah, Dimonah, Adadah, (15:22).
Kedesh, Hazor, Ithnan, (15:23).
Ziph, Telem, Bealoth, (15:24).
Hazor-hadattah, Kerioth-hezron (that is, Hazor), (15:25).
Amam, Shema, Moladah, (15:26).
Hazar-gaddah, Heshmon, Beth-pelet, (15:27).
Hazar-shual, Beersheba, Biziothiah, (15:28).
Baalah, Iim, Ezem, (15:29).
Eltolad, Chesil, Hormah, (15:30).
Ziklag, Madmannah, Sansannah, (15:31).
Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon— twenty-nine cities in all, along with their villages. (15:32).
These were in the foothills: Eshtaol, Zorah, Ashnah, (15:33).
Zanoah, En-gannim, Tappuah, Enam, (15:34).
Jarmuth, Adullam, Socoh, Azekah, (15:35).
Shaaraim, Adithaim, and Gederah (or Gederothaim)— fourteen cities, along with their villages. (15:36).
Zenan, Hadashah, Migdal-gad, (15:37).
Dilan, Mizpeh, Joktheel, (15:38).
Lachish, Bozkath, Eglon, (15:39).
Cabbon, Lahmas, Chitlish, (15:40).
Gederoth, Beth-dagon, Naamah, and Makkedah— sixteen cities, along with their villages. (15:41).
Libnah, Ether, Ashan, (15:42).
Iphtah, Ashnah, Nezib, (15:43).
Keilah, Achzib, and Mareshah— nine cities, along with their villages. (15:44).
Ekron, with its towns and villages; (15:45).
from Ekron to the sea, all the cities near Ashdod, along with their villages; (15:46).
Ashdod, with its towns and villages; Gaza, with its towns and villages, as far as the Brook of Egypt and the coastline of the Great Sea. (15:47).
These were in the hill country: Shamir, Jattir, Socoh, (15:48).
Dannah, Kiriath-sannah (that is, Debir), (15:49).
Anab, Eshtemoh, Anim, (15:50).
Goshen, Holon, and Giloh— eleven cities, along with their villages. (15:51).
Arab, Dumah, Eshan, (15:52).
Janim, Beth-tappuah, Aphekah, (15:53).
Humtah, Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), and Zior— nine cities, along with their villages. (15:54).
Maon, Carmel, Ziph, Juttah, (15:55).
Jezreel, Jokdeam, Zanoah, (15:56).
Kain, Gibeah, and Timnah— ten cities, along with their villages. (15:57).
Halhul, Beth-zur, Gedor, (15:58).
Maarath, Beth-anoth, and Eltekon— six cities, along with their villages. (15:59).
Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), and Rabbah— two cities, along with their villages. (15:60).
These were in the wilderness: Beth-arabah, Middin, Secacah, (15:61).
Nibshan, the City of Salt, and En-gedi— six cities, along with their villages. (15:62).
But the descendants of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem. So to this day the Jebusites live there among the descendants of Judah. (15:63).
crossRefs: Joshua 14:6-15: Caleb's claim on Hebron, granted by Joshua before any of the tribal borders are drawn.
Judges 1:11-15: Othniel takes Kiriath-sepher, and Achsah asks her father for the upper and lower springs.
Judges 1:21: Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites in Jerusalem, and they went on living there together.
2 Samuel 5:6-9: David takes the stronghold of Zion from the Jebusites and names it the city of David.
Genesis 49:8-12: Jacob's blessing on Judah, the lion's cub, whose brothers shall praise him.

translationNotes.note: Verse 21 begins the list of Judah's towns in the Negev. The word means parched land, and because that country lies south of Judah the same word became the ordinary Hebrew word for south. Beersheba on its northern edge gets around eight inches of rain a year, all of it in winter, and there is less further down. It is grazing country with pockets of grain, which is why Achsah asks her father for springs in verse 19 rather than for more acres.

Verse 33 starts the towns of the foothills, and the Hebrew is a proper name for one specific belt of low chalk hills between the Judean ridge and the Philistine coastal plain. Valleys cut through it west to east, and they are the doors into Judah: the Valley of Aijalon (10:12), the Valley of Sorek where Samson met Delilah (Judges 16:4), and the Valley of Elah where David fought Goliath (1 Samuel 17:2). Lachish, Azekah, Socoh and Adullam, all listed in this chapter, are the towns that watch those valleys.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֵּיא בֶן־הִנֹּם (Gei Ben-Hinnom) - Greek: γέεννα (geenna)
translationNotes.note: Verse 8 runs Judah's boundary up this ravine along the south and west sides of Jerusalem. It is where the Tophet stood, the place where children were burned as offerings to Molech; 2 Kings 23:10 says Josiah defiled it so that no one could make his son or daughter pass through the fire, and Jeremiah 7:31 and 32:35 name it again. The Greek form of the valley's name is Gehenna, and that is the word the Gospels render as hell.

translationNotes.term: Kiriath-sepher, the city of the scroll
translationNotes.note: Verse 15 gives Debir's older name, and it means the town of the scroll or of the scribe; verse 49 preserves another form of it, Kiriath-sannah. Names like this were ordinary in Canaan, where every town of any size kept written records on clay and leather and needed men who could write. Othniel takes it in verse 17 and later becomes the first of Israel's judges (Judges 3:9-11).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֻּלֹּת עִלִּיּוֹת וְתַחְתִּיּוֹת (gullot illiyot ve-tahtiyot)
translationNotes.note: Achsah is given land in the Negeb, the dry southern country, and immediately asks for springs as well (verses 18 and 19). In that region a field is worth nothing without water rights, and the springs are the actual gift; the land was only the frame around them. Her request is a piece of practical property law, not sentiment.

stories.keyTakeaway: Judah's tribal boundaries are detailed from the Dead Sea to the Mediterranean, and Joshua grants Caleb his requested portion at Hebron, where Caleb drives out the Anakites and gives his daughter Aksah to Othniel. The chapter then lists Judah's towns by region - the Negev, western foothills, hill country, and wilderness - concluding that the Jebusites remained in Jerusalem despite Judah's settlement.

stories.title: 🗺️ Joshua 16
summaryBullets: The allotment for the descendants of Joseph extended from the Jordan at Jericho to the waters of Jericho on the east, through the wilderness that goes up from Jericho into the hill country of Bethel. (16:1).
It went on from Bethel (that is, Luz) and proceeded to the border of the Archites in Ataroth. (16:2).
Then it descended westward to the border of the Japhletites as far as the border of Lower Beth-horon and on to Gezer, and it ended at the Sea. (16:3).
So Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, received their inheritance. (16:4).
This was the territory of the descendants of Ephraim by their clans: The border of their inheritance went from Ataroth-addar in the east to Upper Beth-horon (16:5).
and out toward the Sea. From Michmethath on the north it turned eastward toward Taanath-shiloh and passed by it to Janoah on the east. (16:6).
From Janoah it went down to Ataroth and Naarah, and then reached Jericho and came out at the Jordan. (16:7).
From Tappuah the border went westward to the Brook of Kanah and ended at the Sea. This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Ephraim, (16:8).
along with all the cities and villages set apart for the descendants of Ephraim within the inheritance of Manasseh. (16:9).
But they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer. So the Canaanites dwell among the Ephraimites to this day, but they are forced laborers. (16:10).
crossRefs: Genesis 48:8-20: Jacob crosses his hands and sets Ephraim, the younger, ahead of Manasseh in the blessing.
Joshua 17:14-18: Joseph's tribes complain their portion is too small and are told to clear the forested hill country.
Judges 1:29: Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, and they remained among them there.
1 Kings 9:16: Pharaoh captures Gezer, burns it, kills its Canaanite inhabitants, and gives it as a dowry to Solomon's wife.
Numbers 26:28-37: The clans of Manasseh and Ephraim counted on the plains of Moab.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית אֵל (Beth El), house of God - לוּז (Luz)
translationNotes.note: Verse 2 gives both names. Luz was the Canaanite town; Jacob renamed the place Bethel, house of God, after the night he slept there with a stone under his head (Genesis 28:11-19). It stands on the ridge road about eleven miles north of Jerusalem, at the boundary between the north and the south, and Jeroboam later set one of his two golden calves there so that northerners would not go down to Jerusalem to worship (1 Kings 12:28-29).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נַחַל קָנָה (Nachal Qanah) - נַחַל (nachal), wadi
translationNotes.note: Verse 8 runs Ephraim's border down this watercourse to the sea. Nachal, translated brook here, means a wadi: a steep-sided channel that carries a torrent in the winter rains and is a dry stony bed the rest of the year. That is why so many tribal borders in these chapters follow one. A wadi does not shift, it can be walked end to end, and it needs no boundary stone that a neighbour could move.

Verse 10 says the Canaanites of Gezer were not driven out but were put to the mas. That is a corvee: a standing obligation to supply work gangs, paid in labour rather than silver, and it is how ancient states got quarrying, hauling and building done. Solomon later put Israelites themselves under a mas of thirty thousand men working in shifts in Lebanon (1 Kings 5:13-14), and the refusal to lighten it is what split the kingdom (1 Kings 12:4-18).

A fortified town on a ridge overlooking the junction of the international coast road with the road climbing east to Jerusalem, about twenty miles northwest of the city. Verse 10 records that Ephraim never took it. A small limestone tablet found there in 1908, the Gezer calendar, lists the farming year month by month and is among the oldest Hebrew inscriptions known.

stories.keyTakeaway: Joseph's descendants, Manasseh and Ephraim, receive their allotted territory, with detailed boundaries for Ephraim's inheritance stretching from the Jordan to the Mediterranean Sea. The Ephraimites fail to drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer, who instead become forced laborers among them.

stories.title: 🗺️ Joshua 17
summaryBullets: Now this was the allotment for the tribe of Manasseh as Joseph’s firstborn son, namely for Machir the firstborn of Manasseh and father of the Gileadites, who had received Gilead and Bashan because Machir was a man of war. (17:1).

So this allotment was for the rest of the descendants of Manasseh — the clans of Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, and Shemida. These are the other male descendants of the clans of Manasseh son of Joseph. (17:2).

But Zelophehad son of Hepher (the son of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh) had no sons but only daughters. These are the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. (17:3).

They approached Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the leaders, and said, “The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers.” So Joshua gave them an inheritance among their father’s brothers, in keeping with the command of the LORD. (17:4).
Thus ten shares fell to Manasseh, in addition to the land of Gilead and Bashan beyond the Jordan, (17:5).
because the daughters of Manasseh received an inheritance among his sons. And the land of Gilead belonged to the rest of the sons of Manasseh. (17:6).
Now the border of Manasseh went from Asher to Michmethath near Shechem, then southward to include the inhabitants of En-tappuah. (17:7).
The region of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but Tappuah itself, on the border of Manasseh, belonged to Ephraim. (17:8).

From there the border continued southward to the Brook of Kanah. There were cities belonging to Ephraim among the cities of Manasseh, but the border of Manasseh was on the north side of the brook and ended at the Sea. (17:9).
Ephraim’s territory was to the south, and Manasseh’s was to the north, having the Sea as its border and adjoining Asher on the north and Issachar on the east. (17:10).
Within Issachar and Asher, Manasseh was assigned Beth-shean, Ibleam, Dor (that is, Naphath), Endor, Taanach, and Megiddo, each with their surrounding settlements. (17:11).
But the descendants of Manasseh were unable to occupy these cities, because the Canaanites were determined to stay in this land. (17:12).
However, when the Israelites grew stronger, they put the Canaanites to forced labor; but they failed to drive them out completely. (17:13).
Then the sons of Joseph said to Joshua, “Why have you given us only one portion as an inheritance? We have many people, because the LORD has blessed us abundantly.” (17:14).

Joshua answered them, “If you have so many people that the hill country of Ephraim is too small for you, go to the forest and clear for yourself an area in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim.” (17:15).
“The hill country is not enough for us,” they replied, “and all the Canaanites who live in the valley have iron chariots, both in Beth-shean with its towns and in the Valley of Jezreel.” (17:16).
So Joshua said to the house of Joseph — to Ephraim and Manasseh — “You have many people and great strength. You shall not have just one allotment, (17:17).

because the hill country will be yours as well. It is a forest; clear it, and its farthest limits will be yours. Although the Canaanites have iron chariots and although they are strong, you can drive them out.” (17:18).
crossRefs: Numbers 27:1-11: Zelophehad's daughters ask for an inheritance, and the law of a daughter's inheritance is given through them.
Numbers 36:1-12: The same daughters must marry within their father's tribe, so that the inheritance does not pass to another tribe.
Judges 1:27-28: Manasseh does not drive out Beth-shan, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam, or Megiddo and their villages.
Judges 4:1-3: The chariots of iron that hold the plain against Israel a generation later.
Deuteronomy 20:1: When you go out to war and see horses and chariots and an army larger than yours, do not be afraid of them.

translationNotes.note: Verse 1 names Machir as Manasseh's firstborn and the father of Gilead, and puts his clan east of the Jordan in Gilead and Bashan because he was a man of war. Machir then stands for the eastern half of the tribe elsewhere in Scripture: Deborah's song calls out the commanders who came down from Machir (Judges 5:14), and Mephibosheth is sheltered by Machir son of Ammiel at Lo-debar (2 Samuel 9:4).

translationNotes.term: The Valley of Jezreel and its ring of towns
translationNotes.note: Verse 11 assigns Manasseh a chain of towns it then cannot take: Beth-shean, Ibleam, Dor, Endor, Taanach and Megiddo. They ring the Jezreel valley, the one broad flat plain in the north, where the international road runs and where the grain grows. Israel holds the hills above it and the Canaanites hold the floor of it, and that standoff is the setting for the wars of Judges 4 to 7 and for Saul's last battle (1 Samuel 29 to 31).

Verses 16 and 18 name the thing that keeps Manasseh out of the plain. A chariot of this period was a light two-wheeled cart on spoked wheels, drawn by a pair of horses, carrying a driver and an archer, with iron worked in where the frame and wheels took the strain. On flat open ground it outruns and outshoots men on foot; on a hillside or in scrub it is useless. Sisera fields nine hundred of them in Judges 4:3, and this is why the Canaanites keep the valleys long after Israel holds the ridges.

Joshua's answer in verses 15 and 18 is to go up into the wooded hill country and cut room out of it. The central highlands carried oak and terebinth woodland then, and settling there meant felling timber, cutting stone terraces into the slopes to hold the soil, and digging cisterns and lining them with plaster because there are few springs on the ridge. He is telling them to do hard labour, not to fight.

Verses 3 to 6 give five women a share of land alongside their uncles. Property normally passed from father to son, and a man with no son left no name on the map; the ruling in Numbers 27:1-11 changed that, and Numbers 36 added that such women must marry inside their own tribe so the land stayed put. This chapter is the ruling being carried out in front of Eleazar and Joshua.

stories.keyTakeaway: Manasseh receives its tribal inheritance, including land east and west of the Jordan; the daughters of Zelophehad are granted their inheritance among male relatives. When Joseph's tribes complain they have insufficient land, Joshua tells them to clear the forested hill country themselves, assuring them they are strong enough to drive out the Canaanites despite their iron chariots.

stories.title: 🗺️ Joshua 18
summaryBullets: Then the whole congregation of Israel assembled at Shiloh and set up the Tent of Meeting there. And though the land was subdued before them, (18:1).
there were still seven tribes of Israel who had not yet received their inheritance. (18:2).
So Joshua said to the Israelites, “How long will you put off entering and possessing the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you? (18:3).
Appoint three men from each tribe, and I will send them out to survey the land and map it out, according to the inheritance of each. Then they will return to me (18:4).
and divide the land into seven portions. Judah shall remain in their territory in the south, and the house of Joseph shall remain in their territory in the north. (18:5).
When you have mapped out the seven portions of land and brought it to me, I will cast lots for you here in the presence of the LORD our God. (18:6).

The Levites, however, have no portion among you, because their inheritance is the priesthood of the LORD. And Gad, Reuben, and half the tribe of Manasseh have already received the inheritance that Moses the servant of the LORD gave them beyond the Jordan to the east.” (18:7).

As the men got up to go out, Joshua commanded them to map out the land, saying, “Go and survey the land, map it out, and return to me. Then I will cast lots for you here in Shiloh in the presence of the LORD.” (18:8).
So the men departed and went throughout the land, mapping it city by city into seven portions. Then they returned with the document to Joshua at the camp in Shiloh. (18:9).
And Joshua cast lots for them in the presence of the LORD at Shiloh, where he distributed the land to the Israelites according to their divisions. (18:10).
The first lot came up for the clans of the tribe of Benjamin. Their allotted territory lay between the tribes of Judah and Joseph: (18:11).
On the north side their border began at the Jordan, went up past the northern slope of Jericho, headed west through the hill country, and came out at the wilderness of Beth-aven. (18:12).
From there the border crossed over to the southern slope of Luz (that is, Bethel) and went down to Ataroth-addar on the hill south of Lower Beth-horon. (18:13).

On the west side the border curved southward from the hill facing Beth-horon on the south and came out at Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), a city of the sons of Judah. This was the western side. (18:14).
On the south side the border began at the outskirts of Kiriath-jearim and extended westward to the spring at the Waters of Nephtoah. (18:15).

Then it went down to the foot of the hill that faces the Valley of Ben-hinnom at the northern end of the Valley of Rephaim and ran down the Valley of Hinnom toward the southern slope of the Jebusites and downward to En-rogel. (18:16).
From there it curved northward and proceeded to En-shemesh and on to Geliloth facing the Ascent of Adummim, and continued down to the Stone of Bohan son of Reuben. (18:17).
Then it went on to the northern slope of Beth-arabah and went down into the valley. (18:18).
The border continued to the northern slope of Beth-hoglah and came out at the northern bay of the Salt Sea, at the mouth of the Jordan. This was the southern border. (18:19).
On the east side the border was the Jordan. These were the borders around the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Benjamin. (18:20).
These were the cities of the clans of the tribe of Benjamin: Jericho, Beth-hoglah, Emek-keziz, (18:21).
Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, Bethel, (18:22).
Avvim, Parah, Ophrah, (18:23).
Chephar-ammoni, Ophni, and Geba— twelve cities, along with their villages. (18:24).
Gibeon, Ramah, Beeroth, (18:25).
Mizpeh, Chephirah, Mozah, (18:26).
Rekem, Irpeel, Taralah, (18:27).
Zelah, Haeleph, Jebus (that is, Jerusalem), Gibeah, and Kiriath-jearim— fourteen cities, along with their villages. This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Benjamin. (18:28).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 1:3,9: Elkanah goes up year by year to worship at Shiloh, where Eli sat on his seat by the doorpost of the temple of the LORD.
Judges 21:19: The yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh, north of Bethel, east of the highway, and south of Lebonah.
Jeremiah 7:12-14: Go now to My place at Shiloh, where I made My name dwell at the first, and see what I did to it.
Psalm 78:60: He forsook the dwelling at Shiloh, the tent where He had dwelt among mankind.
Proverbs 16:33: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.

translationNotes.note: Verses 6, 8 and 10 have Joshua cast lots at Shiloh in the presence of the LORD. Lots were marked stones or sherds shaken in a fold of cloth or in a vessel until one came out, and Proverbs 16:33 states the principle behind the practice: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD. The same method finds Achan (7:16-18), picks Saul (1 Samuel 10:20-21), orders the priestly courses (1 Chronicles 24:5) and settles the two goats on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:8). It also means no tribe can accuse Joshua, an Ephraimite, of drawing the lines to suit his own people.

Verse 1 sets the tent of meeting up at Shiloh, in the hill country of Ephraim about twenty miles north of Jerusalem, and it stays there for the whole period of the judges. This is where Hannah prayed and Samuel grew up, and the ark left it and never came back when the Philistines took it (1 Samuel 4). Jeremiah 7:12-14 points back to Shiloh's ruin as the standing warning that God can give up a place He once named as His own.

translationNotes.term: Wrote it down in a book
translationNotes.note: Verses 4 to 9 send three men from each tribe to walk the remaining land, write a survey of it town by town, and bring the document back. Land was allotted from a written description and then assigned by lot before the LORD, so no tribe could claim it had been cheated by whoever drew the lines. The seven portions in this chapter come out of that survey.

Verse 28 lists Jebus among Benjamin's towns and notes that it is Jerusalem; 15:63 has already said Judah could not drive the Jebusites out of it. The town sat on a narrow spur between two ravines with the Gihon spring at its foot, which is what made it defensible and what let it hold out through the whole book. It stayed Jebusite until David took it, and it then belonged to neither Judah nor Benjamin but to the king (2 Samuel 5:6-9).

stories.keyTakeaway: The assembly gathers at Shiloh; Joshua directs three men from each of the seven remaining tribes to survey and map the land, then casts lots to distribute territories, with Benjamin receiving the first allotment between Judah and Joseph.

stories.title: 🗺️ Joshua 19

Their territory included Helkath, Hali, Beten, Achshaph, (19:25).
Allammelech, Amad, and Mishal. On the west the border touched Carmel and Shihor-libnath, (19:26).
then turned eastward toward Beth-dagon, touched Zebulun and the Valley of Iphtah-el, and went north to Beth-emek and Neiel, passing Cabul on the left. (19:27).
It went on to Ebron, Rehob, Hammon, and Kanah, as far as Greater Sidon. (19:28).
The border then turned back toward Ramah as far as the fortified city of Tyre, turned toward Hosah, and came out at the Sea in the region of Achzib, (19:29).

This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Asher, including these cities and their villages. (19:31).
The sixth lot came out for the clans of the tribe of Naphtali: (19:32).
Their border started at Heleph and the great tree of Zaanannim, passing Adami-nekeb and Jabneel as far as Lakkum and ending at the Jordan. (19:33).
Then the border turned westward to Aznoth-tabor and ran from there to Hukkok, touching Zebulun on the south side, Asher on the west, and Judah at the Jordan on the east. (19:34).
The fortified cities were Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, Chinnereth, (19:35).
Adamah, Ramah, Hazor, (19:36).
Kedesh, Edrei, En-hazor, (19:37).
Iron, Migdal-el, Horem, Beth-anath, and Beth-shemesh. There were nineteen cities, along with their villages. (19:38).
This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Naphtali, including these cities and their villages. (19:39).
The seventh lot came out for the clans of the tribe of Dan: (19:40).
The territory of their inheritance included Zorah, Eshtaol, Ir-shemesh, (19:41).
Shaalabbin, Aijalon, Ithlah, (19:42).
Elon, Timnah, Ekron, (19:43).
Eltekeh, Gibbethon, Baalath, (19:44).
Jehud, Bene-berak, Gath-rimmon, (19:45).
Me-jarkon, and Rakkon, including the territory across from Joppa. (19:46).

(Later, when the territory of the Danites was lost to them, they went up and fought against Leshem, captured it, and put it to the sword. So they took possession of Leshem, settled there, and renamed it after their father Dan.) (19:47).
This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Dan, including these cities and their villages. (19:48).
When they had finished distributing the land into its territories, the Israelites gave Joshua son of Nun an inheritance among them, (19:49).
as the LORD had commanded. They gave him the city of Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim, as he requested. He rebuilt the city and settled in it. (19:50).

These are the inheritances that Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the heads of the families distributed by lot to the tribes of Israel at Shiloh before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. So they finished dividing up the land. (19:51).
crossRefs: Genesis 49:5-7: Simeon and Levi are to be divided in Jacob and scattered in Israel.
Joshua 21:9-16: Towns for the priests are taken out of Judah and Simeon, inside the same southern territory.
Judges 1:34: The Amorites press the people of Dan back into the hill country and will not let them come down to the plain.
Judges 18:1-31: Dan sends out spies, takes Laish in the far north, and renames the town Dan.
Matthew 4:13-16: The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, Galilee of the Gentiles, where the people saw a great light.

translationNotes.note: Verses 1 and 9 give Simeon no block of its own. Its towns sit inside Judah's southern territory because Judah's share had been drawn too large, and the tribe is steadily absorbed; by the time of the kings Simeon has almost stopped appearing as a separate people. Jacob had said of Simeon and Levi that he would divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel (Genesis 49:7), and both tribes end up living inside other men's land.

Verse 13 puts this village on Zebulun's border in the hills of lower Galilee, a few miles north-east of Nazareth. It is the home town of the prophet Jonah son of Amittai, named as such at 2 Kings 14:25, where he foretells Jeroboam II restoring Israel's northern border. The man sent to Nineveh came from a hill village in Galilee.

Verse 22 sets Tabor on Issachar's border, at the point where Issachar, Zebulun and Naphtali meet. It is a bare dome of a hill rising about 1,886 feet straight out of the flat Jezreel plain, steep on every side and visible from a long way off. Barak musters ten thousand men on it and comes down off it into Sisera's chariots (Judges 4:6-14), which is the whole of the tactic: chariots cannot climb it and cannot fight on the slope.

Verses 40 to 46 give Dan a small allotment on the coastal plain, squeezed between Judah, Ephraim and the Philistine towns of Ekron and Timnah, and verse 47 records that the tribe lost it and went north instead. They took Leshem by the sword and renamed it Dan after their ancestor. Judges 18 tells the same migration at length and calls the town Laish; it sits at the far north of the country over the largest spring feeding the Jordan, and from then on the phrase from Dan to Beersheba means the whole land.

Verses 49 and 50 give Joshua his portion last, after every tribe has been served, and he asks for one particular town in the hill country of Ephraim instead of drawing it by lot. Verse 50 says he had to rebuild it before he could live in it. He is buried there at the end of the book (24:30).

stories.keyTakeaway: The remaining northern tribes receive their allotted territories: Simeon within Judah's borders, followed by Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan, with specified town lists and boundaries for each. Joshua is then given Timnath Serah in the hill country of Ephraim, completing the land division overseen by Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal leaders at Shiloh.

stories.title: 🗺️ Joshua 20
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Joshua, (20:1).
“Tell the Israelites to designate the cities of refuge, as I instructed you through Moses, (20:2).
so that anyone who kills another unintentionally or accidentally may flee there. These will be your refuge from the avenger of blood. (20:3).

When someone flees to one of these cities, stands at the entrance of the city gate, and states his case before its elders, they are to bring him into the city and give him a place to live among them. (20:4).
Now if the avenger of blood pursues him, they must not surrender the manslayer into his hand, because that man killed his neighbor accidentally without prior malice. (20:5).

He is to stay in that city until he stands trial before the assembly and until the death of the high priest serving at that time. Then the manslayer may return to his own home in the city from which he fled.” (20:6).
So they set apart Kedesh in Galilee in the hill country of Naphtali, Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the hill country of Judah. (20:7).

And beyond the Jordan, east of Jericho, they designated Bezer on the wilderness plateau from the tribe of Reuben, Ramoth in Gilead from the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan from the tribe of Manasseh. (20:8).

These are the cities appointed for all the Israelites and foreigners among them, so that anyone who kills a person unintentionally may flee there and not die by the hand of the avenger of blood prior to standing trial before the assembly. (20:9).
crossRefs: Numbers 35:9-34: The full law of the cities of refuge, the trial before the assembly, and the death of the high priest.
Deuteronomy 19:1-13: Three cities are set apart with roads prepared, so that the manslayer can reach one and live.
Deuteronomy 4:41-43: Moses sets apart Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan east of the Jordan before he dies.
Exodus 21:12-14: Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall be put to death, but for one who did not lie in wait a place is appointed.
Deuteronomy 19:15-21: A charge stands only on two or three witnesses, and the judges are to inquire diligently.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עִיר מִקְלָט (ir miqlat), town of asylum
translationNotes.note: Six towns set apart so that a man who killed without intent could run to one and stand trial instead of being cut down at the roadside. The law behind it is Numbers 35:9-34 and Deuteronomy 19:1-13, and it grades killing by intent exactly as modern law does. An iron object, a stone in the hand that could kill, a wooden weapon, shoving in hatred, or hurling something while lying in wait make it murder (Numbers 35:16-21); no enmity, no ambush, and not seeing the man make it manslaughter (35:22-23). Deuteronomy 19:5 gives the worked example, an axe head flying off the handle.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֹּאֵל הַדָּם (goel ha-dam), redeemer of blood
translationNotes.note: There was no police force and no public prosecutor. When a man was killed, the duty of pursuing the killer fell on his nearest male relative, the goel, the same word used for the kinsman who buys back family land or a family member sold into debt. Numbers 35:19 says the goel ha-dam shall himself put the murderer to death. The cities of refuge exist because that system, left alone, killed men who had not murdered anyone.

translationNotes.term: Stating his case at the gate
translationNotes.note: Verse 4 has the man stop at the entrance of the city gate and lay out his case in the hearing of the elders before they will take him in. The gate was the courthouse. Town gates were built as a walled passage with chambers and stone benches down each side, the one place everyone passed and business could be witnessed, and that is where legal matters were done: Boaz settles the redemption of Ruth at the gate and seats ten elders there (Ruth 4:1-2), Deuteronomy 21:19 sends a case to the elders at the gate, and Amos 5:15 tells Israel to establish justice in the gate.

Verses 7 and 8 name all six: Kedesh in Galilee, Shechem in the hills of Ephraim, and Hebron in Judah on the west side; Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead, and Golan in Bashan on the east. Bezer is a town on the open tableland of Reuben, east of the Dead Sea. Three each side, spread north to south, so that no one in the land was more than a hard day from a place where he could stand trial instead of being cut down at the roadside.

translationNotes.term: Until the death of the high priest
translationNotes.note: Verse 6 sets the term: the man stays in the city until he has stood trial and then until the high priest of that time dies, after which he may go home free (Numbers 35:25-28). It is not a prison sentence with a fixed length; it ends with a death that has nothing to do with him. Outside the city's boundary the avenger could still lawfully kill him.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Lord commands Joshua to establish six cities of refuge where anyone who kills someone accidentally can flee for protection; the Israelites designate Kedesh, Shechem, and Hebron west of the Jordan, and Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan east of it.

stories.title: 🗺️ Joshua 21
summaryBullets: Now the family heads of the Levites approached Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the heads of the other tribes of Israel (21:1).

So by the command of the LORD, the Israelites gave the Levites these cities and their pasturelands out of their own inheritance: (21:3).
The first lot came out for the Kohathite clans. The Levites who were descendants of Aaron the priest received thirteen cities by lot from the tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin. (21:4).
The remaining descendants of Kohath received ten cities by lot from the tribes of Ephraim, Dan, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. (21:5).
The descendants of Gershon received thirteen cities by lot from the tribes of Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and the half-tribe of Manasseh in Bashan. (21:6).
And the descendants of Merari received twelve cities from the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Zebulun. (21:7).
So the Israelites allotted to the Levites these cities, together with their pasturelands, as the LORD had commanded through Moses. (21:8).
From the tribes of Judah and Simeon, they designated these cities by name (21:9).
to the descendants of Aaron from the Kohathite clans of the Levites, because the first lot fell to them: (21:10).
They gave them Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), with its surrounding pasturelands, in the hill country of Judah. (Arba was the father of Anak.) (21:11).

Holon, Debir, (21:15).

Kibzaim, and Beth-horon— four cities, together with their pasturelands. (21:22).

From the tribe of Issachar they were given Kishion, Daberath, (21:28).
Jarmuth, and En-gannim— four cities, together with their pasturelands. (21:29).
From the tribe of Asher they were given Mishal, Abdon, (21:30).
Helkath, and Rehob— four cities, together with their pasturelands. (21:31).
And from the tribe of Naphtali they were given Kedesh in Galilee (a city of refuge for the manslayer), Hammoth-dor, and Kartan— three cities, together with their pasturelands. (21:32).
In all, thirteen cities, together with their pasturelands, were given to the Gershonite clans. (21:33).
This is what the Merarite clan (the rest of the Levites) were given: From the tribe of Zebulun they were given Jokneam, Kartah, (21:34).
Dimnah, and Nahalal— four cities, together with their pasturelands. (21:35).
From the tribe of Reuben they were given Bezer, Jahaz, (21:36).
