And from the tribe of Gad they were given Ramoth in Gilead, a city of refuge for the manslayer, Mahanaim, (21:38).
Heshbon, and Jazer— four cities in all, together with their pasturelands. (21:39).
In all, twelve cities were allotted to the clans of Merari, the remaining Levite clans. (21:40).
For the Levites, then, there were forty-eight cities in all, together with their pasturelands, within the territory of the Israelites. (21:41).
Each of these cities had its own surrounding pasturelands; this was true for all the cities. (21:42).
Thus the LORD gave Israel all the land He had sworn to give their fathers, and they took possession of it and settled in it. (21:43).
And the LORD gave them rest on every side, just as He had sworn to their fathers. None of their enemies could stand against them, for the LORD delivered all their enemies into their hand. (21:44).
Not one of all the LORD’s good promises to the house of Israel had failed; everything was fulfilled. (21:45).
crossRefs: Numbers 35:1-8: Give the Levites towns to live in and pasturelands around them, forty-eight towns in all.
Genesis 49:5-7: Simeon and Levi will be divided in Jacob and scattered in Israel.
Numbers 18:20-24: The LORD is Levi's portion and inheritance, and the tithes of Israel are given them for their service.
Deuteronomy 18:1-2: The priests and the whole tribe of Levi shall have no portion or inheritance along with Israel.
1 Chronicles 6:54-81: The same list of Levitical towns, set out family by family in the Chronicler's record.

translationNotes.note: Verses 4 to 7 divide the towns among Levi's three clans, named after Levi's three sons. Each had carried a different part of the tabernacle on the march: Kohath the ark and the holy furniture, on their shoulders and never on a cart (Numbers 4:4-15, 7:9); Gershon the curtains, coverings and hangings; Merari the frames, bars, pillars and bases (Numbers 4:24-33). Aaron's line, the priests, is one family inside Kohath, and verses 4 and 10 give them the towns nearest Jerusalem in Judah, Simeon and Benjamin.

Verse 41 totals the Levites' towns at forty-eight, the number Numbers 35:7 had commanded, and six of them are the cities of refuge named in the previous chapter. The tribe with no territory of its own is planted inside every other tribe's territory instead, from Kedesh in the far north to the Negev towns in the south. Wherever a man lived there were Levites within reach whose work included teaching him the law (Deuteronomy 33:10).

Verse 18 hands this small priestly town in Benjamin to Aaron's descendants; it stands about three miles north-east of Jerusalem. Solomon banished the priest Abiathar to his fields there rather than executing him (1 Kings 2:26). Jeremiah was a priest of Anathoth (Jeremiah 1:1), and while Jerusalem was under siege he bought a field there for seventeen shekels of silver as a signed and witnessed sign that land in Judah would be worth owning again (Jeremiah 32:6-15).

A male descendant of Levi (excluding the Aaronic priestly line). Assisted the priests in temple service: music, gatekeeping, instructing the people, preparing sacrifices. The priest and Levite who pass by the wounded man in the Good Samaritan parable (Luke 10:31-32) make Jesus' point cut sharper; both were professionally obligated to help.

A Levitical town came with open ground around it for the households' animals, not with farmland. Numbers 35:4 measures that ground as reaching a thousand cubits out from the wall, about 1,500 feet, and 35:5 measures two thousand cubits along each side. Levi lived off the offerings and tithes, so the towns gave the tribe somewhere to live in every part of Israel without giving it a territory of its own.

stories.keyTakeaway: Levite family heads request towns and pasturelands as commanded by the LORD; Israel distributes forty-eight towns across the tribes, with specific allocations to the Kohathite, Gershonite, and Merarite clans. The LORD fulfills his promises by giving Israel all the land he swore to their ancestors and bringing them rest from their enemies.

stories.title: 🤝 Joshua 22
summaryBullets: Then Joshua summoned the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh (22:1).
and told them, “You have done all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, and you have obeyed my voice in all that I commanded you. (22:2).
All this time you have not deserted your brothers, up to this very day, but have kept the charge given you by the LORD your God. (22:3).
And now that the LORD your God has given your brothers rest as He promised them, you may return to your homes in the land that Moses the servant of the LORD gave you across the Jordan. (22:4).

But be very careful to observe the commandment and the law that Moses the servant of the LORD gave you: to love the LORD your God, to walk in all His ways, to keep His commandments, to hold fast to Him, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul.” (22:5).
So Joshua blessed them and sent them on their way, and they went to their homes. (22:6).

(To the half-tribe of Manasseh Moses had given land in Bashan, and to the other half Joshua gave land on the west side of the Jordan among their brothers.) When Joshua sent them to their homes he blessed them, (22:7).

saying, “Return to your homes with your great wealth, with immense herds of livestock, with silver, gold, bronze, iron, and very many clothes. Divide with your brothers the spoil of your enemies.” (22:8).

So the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh left the Israelites at Shiloh in the land of Canaan to return to their own land of Gilead, which they had acquired according to the command of the LORD through Moses. (22:9).
And when they came to Geliloth near the Jordan in the land of Canaan, the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh built an imposing altar there by the Jordan. (22:10).

Then the Israelites received the report: “Behold, the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh have built an altar on the border of the land of Canaan, at Geliloth near the Jordan on the Israelite side.” (22:11).
And when they heard this, the whole congregation of Israel assembled at Shiloh to go to war against them. (22:12).
The Israelites sent Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest to the land of Gilead, to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. (22:13).
With him they sent ten chiefs — one family leader from each tribe of Israel, each the head of a family among the clans of Israel. (22:14).
They went to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh in the land of Gilead and said to them, (22:15).

“This is what the whole congregation of the LORD says: ‘What is this breach of faith you have committed today against the God of Israel by turning away from the LORD and building for yourselves an altar, that you might rebel against the LORD this day? (22:16).
Was not the sin of Peor enough for us, from which we have not cleansed ourselves to this day? It even brought a plague upon the congregation of the LORD. (22:17).
And now, would you turn away from the LORD? If you rebel today against the LORD, tomorrow He will be angry with the whole congregation of Israel. (22:18).

If indeed the land of your inheritance is unclean, then cross over to the land of the LORD’s possession, where the LORD’s tabernacle stands, and take possession of it among us. But do not rebel against the LORD or against us by building for yourselves an altar other than the altar of the LORD our God. (22:19).

Was not Achan son of Zerah unfaithful regarding what was set apart for destruction, bringing wrath upon the whole congregation of Israel? Yet it was not only Achan who perished because of his sin!’” (22:20).
Then the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh answered the leaders of the clans of Israel: (22:21).
“The LORD, the Mighty One, is God! The LORD, the Mighty One, is God! He knows, and may Israel also know. If this was in rebellion or breach of faith against the LORD, do not spare us today. (22:22).

If we have built for ourselves an altar to turn away from Him and to offer burnt offerings and grain offerings on it, or to sacrifice peace offerings on it, may the LORD Himself hold us accountable. (22:23).
But in fact we have done this for fear that in the future your descendants might say to ours, ‘What have you to do with the LORD, the God of Israel? (22:24).
For the LORD has made the Jordan a border between us and you Reubenites and Gadites. You have no share in the LORD!’ So your descendants could cause ours to stop fearing the LORD. (22:25).
That is why we said, ‘Let us take action and build an altar for ourselves, but not for burnt offerings or sacrifices. (22:26).

Rather, let it be a witness between us and you and the generations to come, that we will worship the LORD in His presence with our burnt offerings, sacrifices, and peace offerings.’ Then in the future, your descendants cannot say to ours, ‘You have no share in the LORD!’ (22:27).

Therefore we said, ‘If they ever say this to us or to our descendants, we will answer: Look at the replica of the altar of the LORD that our fathers made, not for burnt offerings or sacrifices, but as a witness between us and you.’ (22:28).

Far be it from us to rebel against the LORD and turn away from Him today by building an altar for burnt offerings, grain offerings, or sacrifices, other than the altar of the LORD our God, which stands before His tabernacle.” (22:29).

When Phinehas the priest and the chiefs of the congregation — the heads of Israel’s clans who were with him — heard what the descendants of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh had to say, they were satisfied. (22:30).

Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest said to the descendants of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh, “Today we know that the LORD is among us, because you have not committed this breach of faith against Him. Consequently, you have delivered the Israelites from the hand of the LORD.” (22:31).

Then Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest, together with the other leaders, returned to the Israelites in the land of Canaan and brought back a report regarding the Reubenites and Gadites in the land of Gilead. (22:32).
The Israelites were satisfied with the report, and they blessed God and spoke no more about going to war against them to destroy the land where the Reubenites and Gadites lived. (22:33).
So the Reubenites and Gadites named the altar Witness, for they said, “It is a witness between us that the LORD is God.” (22:34).
crossRefs: Numbers 32:20-33: The eastern tribes promise to cross over armed and not go home until Israel has its inheritance.
Deuteronomy 12:13-14: Do not offer your burnt offerings at any place you see, but only at the place the LORD chooses.
Leviticus 17:8-9: Anyone who offers a burnt offering and does not bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting shall be cut off.
Numbers 25:1-9: The plague at Peor that Phinehas stopped, which he brings up against them in verse 17.
Joshua 7:1-26: Achan's unfaithfulness brings wrath on the whole congregation, the precedent named in verse 20.

translationNotes.note: Verse 34 names the altar Ed, witness. Under the law a matter is established by two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and where no person can testify an object is set up to do it: the heap of stones between Jacob and Laban (Genesis 31:48), the stone Joshua sets up at Shechem (24:26-27), and this altar. It is built to be pointed at and argued from, never sacrificed on, which is the whole of the eastern tribes' defence in verses 26 to 29.

Verse 17 asks whether the sin of Peor was not enough, and expects every hearer to know what that was. Numbers 25:1-9: Israel, camped at Shittim, joined Moabite and Midianite women in eating the sacrifices of their god and bowing down to him; a plague broke out and killed twenty-four thousand, and it stopped when Phinehas drove a spear through an Israelite man and a Midianite woman inside the tent. Phinehas is the man Israel sends to confront the eastern tribes in verse 13, which is why they answer him so carefully.

The word the delegation uses in verses 16, 20, 22 and 31 is maal, not the ordinary word for sin. It means treachery against what is holy: taking or misusing something that belongs to God. It is the charge laid against Achan at 7:1, and Leviticus 5:15 uses it of trespass against the holy things. They are not accusing the eastern tribes of a lapse but of robbing God, which is why the whole congregation musters for war in verse 12.

Deuteronomy 12:5-14 confines burnt offerings and sacrifices to the one place the LORD chooses to put His name and forbids offering them wherever a man pleases. That law is what makes a second altar look like rebellion rather than devotion, and it is the charge the eastern tribes answer in verses 26 to 29: the structure is a copy of the altar, built as a witness, and nothing will ever be offered on it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Joshua dismisses the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh to their eastern lands with his blessing; when they build an altar at the Jordan's border, the other Israelites prepare for war until Phinehas and tribal leaders learn the altar is a memorial to affirm their covenant loyalty, not for sacrifices.

stories.title: 🤝 Joshua 23
summaryBullets: A long time after the LORD had given Israel rest from all the enemies around them, when Joshua was old and well along in years, (23:1).
he summoned all Israel, including its elders, leaders, judges, and officers. “I am old and well along in years,” he said, (23:2).
“and you have seen everything that the LORD your God has done to all these nations for your sake, because it was the LORD your God who fought for you. (23:3).
See, I have allotted as an inheritance to your tribes these remaining nations, including all the nations I have already cut off, from the Jordan westward to the Great Sea. (23:4).
The LORD your God will push them out of your way and drive them out before you, so that you can take possession of their land, as the LORD your God promised you. (23:5).
Be very strong, then, so that you can keep and obey all that is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, not turning aside from it to the right or to the left. (23:6).
So you are not to associate with these nations that remain among you. You must not call on the names of their gods or swear by them, and you must not serve them or bow down to them. (23:7).
Instead, you shall hold fast to the LORD your God, as you have done to this day. (23:8).
The LORD has driven out great and powerful nations before you, and to this day no one can stand against you. (23:9).
One of you can put a thousand to flight, because the LORD your God fights for you, just as He promised. (23:10).
Therefore watch yourselves carefully, that you love the LORD your God. (23:11).
For if you turn away and cling to the rest of these nations that remain among you, and if you intermarry and associate with them, (23:12).

know for sure that the LORD your God will no longer drive out these nations before you. Instead, they will become for you a snare and a trap, a scourge in your sides and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from this good land that the LORD your God has given you. (23:13).

Now behold, today I am going the way of all the earth, and you know with all your heart and soul that not one of the good promises the LORD your God made to you has failed. Everything was fulfilled for you; not one promise has failed. (23:14).

But just as every good thing the LORD your God promised you has come to pass, likewise the LORD will bring upon you the calamity He has threatened, until He has destroyed you from this good land He has given you. (23:15).

If you transgress the covenant of the LORD your God, which He commanded you, and go and serve other gods and bow down to them, then the anger of the LORD will burn against you, and you will quickly perish from this good land He has given you.” (23:16).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 7:1-5: Make no covenant with them, do not intermarry with them, and tear down their altars, pillars, and Asherim.
Exodus 23:31-33: They shall not dwell in your land, or they will make you sin against Me, for their gods will be a snare to you.
Numbers 33:55: Those you let remain shall be barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides, and they shall trouble you in the land.
Judges 2:1-3: The angel at Bochim says the nations left will be thorns in their sides and their gods a snare, exactly as warned here.
Deuteronomy 28:63: As the LORD took delight in doing you good, so He will take delight in bringing ruin on you and plucking you off the land.

translationNotes.note: Four separate offices are being summoned. The elders were the heads of families who sat in the gate and decided cases; the heads were the tribal and clan chiefs; the judges settled disputes; and the shoterim were the record-keeping officials who mustered men, kept lists, and passed down orders. The word first appears in Exodus 5:6-19, where the Israelite shoterim are the foremen beaten by the Egyptian taskmasters over the brick quota.

translationNotes.term: Do not call on the names of their gods
translationNotes.note: Baal means lord, and he was the Canaanite storm god who was held to give the rain the whole harvest depended on; his prophets on Carmel cut themselves with swords and lances until the blood ran (1 Kings 18:28). Asherah was a goddess, and the asherah named in the law is her cult object, a wooden pole or living tree planted beside an altar (Deuteronomy 16:21); Gideon cut his father's down and burned it under the sacrifice (Judges 6:25-26). Exodus 23:13 forbids even letting the names of such gods be heard on an Israelite's lips.

translationNotes.term: One of you can put a thousand to flight
translationNotes.note: Joshua is quoting terms already set out in the law. Leviticus 26:8 promises that five will chase a hundred and a hundred will chase ten thousand if Israel keeps the covenant, and Deuteronomy 32:30 puts the reverse case: how could one chase a thousand unless their Rock had sold them. Verse 10 states the promise; verses 15 and 16 state the other half.

Deuteronomy 7:3-4 gives the stated reason for the ban: the foreign wife turns the son away to serve other gods. Solomon is the worked example. 1 Kings 11:1-8 lists what his wives brought in: Ashtoreth of the Sidonians, Chemosh of Moab, and Molech of Ammon, with high places built for them east of Jerusalem. Chemosh received human sacrifice, and 2 Kings 3:27 records the king of Moab offering his eldest son as a burnt offering on the city wall; the Moabite Stone, an inscription of that same King Mesha from about 840 BC, credits Chemosh with his victories over Israel.

translationNotes.term: A scourge in your sides and thorns in your eyes
translationNotes.note: The first two words in the list are trapping equipment: a pach is the bird trap, a net that springs shut, and a moqesh is the baited trigger stick that sets it off. The warning is a direct quotation of the sentence already passed in Numbers 33:55, that those left in the land will become barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides.

stories.keyTakeaway: An elderly Joshua assembles Israel's leaders and warns them to obey the Law of Moses, avoid associating with remaining nations, and stay faithful to the LORD; he reminds them that God has kept all his promises and will bring curses if they turn to other gods.

stories.title: 🤝 Joshua 24
summaryBullets: Then Joshua assembled all the tribes of Israel at Shechem. He summoned the elders, leaders, judges, and officers of Israel, and they presented themselves before God. (24:1).

And Joshua said to all the people, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Long ago your fathers, including Terah the father of Abraham and Nahor, lived beyond the Euphrates and worshiped other gods. (24:2).
But I took your father Abraham from beyond the Euphrates and led him through all the land of Canaan, and I multiplied his descendants. I gave him Isaac, (24:3).
and to Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau. I gave Esau Mount Seir to possess, but Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt. (24:4).
Then I sent Moses and Aaron, and I afflicted the Egyptians by what I did there, and afterward I brought you out. (24:5).
When I brought your fathers out of Egypt and you reached the Red Sea, the Egyptians pursued them with chariots and horsemen as far as the Red Sea. (24:6).

So your fathers cried out to the LORD, and He put darkness between you and the Egyptians, over whom He brought the sea and engulfed them. Your very eyes saw what I did to the Egyptians. Then you lived in the wilderness for a long time. (24:7).

Later, I brought you to the land of the Amorites who lived beyond the Jordan. They fought against you, but I delivered them into your hand, that you should possess their land when I destroyed them before you. (24:8).
Then Balak son of Zippor, the king of Moab, set out to fight against Israel. He sent for Balaam son of Beor to curse you, (24:9).
but I would not listen to Balaam. So he blessed you again and again, and I delivered you from his hand. (24:10).

After this, you crossed the Jordan and came to Jericho. The people of Jericho fought against you, as did the Amorites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hittites, Girgashites, Hivites, and Jebusites, and I delivered them into your hand. (24:11).
I sent the hornet ahead of you, and it drove out the two Amorite kings before you, but not by your own sword or bow. (24:12).
So I gave you a land on which you did not toil and cities that you did not build, and now you live in them and eat from vineyards and olive groves that you did not plant.’ (24:13).
Now, therefore, fear the LORD and serve Him in sincerity and truth; cast aside the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt, and serve the LORD. (24:14).

But if it is unpleasing in your sight to serve the LORD, then choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you are living. As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!” (24:15).
The people replied, “Far be it from us to forsake the LORD to serve other gods! (24:16).

For the LORD our God brought us and our fathers out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, and performed these great signs before our eyes. He also protected us throughout our journey and among all the nations through which we traveled. (24:17).
And the LORD drove out before us all the nations, including the Amorites who lived in the land. We too will serve the LORD, because He is our God!” (24:18).
But Joshua said to the people, “You are not able to serve the LORD, for He is a holy God; He is a jealous God; He will not forgive your rebellion or your sins. (24:19).
If you forsake the LORD and serve foreign gods, He will turn and bring disaster on you and consume you, even after He has been good to you.” (24:20).
“No!” replied the people. “We will serve the LORD!” (24:21).
Then Joshua told them, “You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen to serve the LORD.” “We are witnesses!” they said. (24:22).
“Now, therefore,” he said, “get rid of the foreign gods among you and incline your hearts to the LORD, the God of Israel.” (24:23).
So the people said to Joshua, “We will serve the LORD our God and obey His voice.” (24:24).
On that day Joshua made a covenant for the people, and there at Shechem he established for them a statute and ordinance. (24:25).
Joshua recorded these things in the Book of the Law of God. Then he took a large stone and set it up there under the oak that was near the sanctuary of the LORD. (24:26).

And Joshua said to all the people, “You see this stone. It will be a witness against us, for it has heard all the words the LORD has spoken to us, and it will be a witness against you if you ever deny your God.” (24:27).
Then Joshua sent the people away, each to his own inheritance. (24:28).
Some time later, Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of 110. (24:29).
And they buried him in the land of his inheritance, at Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash. (24:30).
Israel had served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him and who had experienced all the works that the LORD had done for Israel. (24:31).

And the bones of Joseph, which the Israelites had brought up out of Egypt, were buried at Shechem in the plot of land that Jacob had purchased from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for a hundred pieces of silver. So it became an inheritance for Joseph’s descendants. (24:32).
Eleazar son of Aaron also died, and they buried him at Gibeah, which had been given to his son Phinehas in the hill country of Ephraim. (24:33).
crossRefs: Genesis 12:1-7: The LORD calls Abram out and promises the land to his offspring, the history verse 3 begins from.
Genesis 35:2-4: Jacob tells his household to put away the foreign gods, and buries them under the oak at Shechem.
Genesis 50:24-26: Joseph makes the sons of Israel swear to carry his bones up out of Egypt when God visits them.
Exodus 13:19: Moses takes the bones of Joseph with him out of Egypt, because of the oath Joseph had made them swear.
Genesis 33:18-20: Jacob buys the piece of ground at Shechem for a hundred pieces of money and sets up an altar there.

translationNotes.note: A berit is a binding agreement with sanctions, sworn in public and put in writing, and this chapter runs through the standard shape of one in order: who the maker is and what He has done (verses 2 to 13), what is required (14 and 23), the answer of the other party (16 to 18, 21 to 24), the terms written down (25 and 26), and a witness set up (26 and 27). Verse 25 uses the ordinary Hebrew idiom, Joshua cut a covenant, which comes from the practice of cutting animals in two and passing between the pieces (Genesis 15:9-18, Jeremiah 34:18).

The word running through verses 14 to 24 is avad, to serve or to work for; it is used of a slave's labour and of a farmer working ground. Joshua is not asking which god they feel warmly about but which one they will take orders from and bring offerings to, which is why verse 15 offers a choice between three named masters: the gods of Mesopotamia, the gods of Egypt, and the gods of the Amorites. Exodus 3:12 uses the same word for Israel serving God at the mountain, and Exodus 20:5 forbids serving carved images.

Verses 26 and 27 set a large stone under the oak at the sanctuary, and Joshua says it has heard everything and will testify against them. A standing stone was the ordinary way to make an agreement permanent and public in a world where almost nobody read: Jacob and Laban raise one (Genesis 31:45-52), and Samuel sets up Ebenezer after Mizpah (1 Samuel 7:12). It is a legal record that cannot be lost, altered, or claimed never to have existed.

Verses 2, 14, and 15 speak of the gods your fathers served beyond the River, meaning the Euphrates, in Mesopotamia where Abraham came from. Joshua names three sets of gods Israel could choose: those of Mesopotamia, those of Egypt, and those of the Amorites whose land they now live in. Verse 2 says plainly that Terah, Abraham's own father, served other gods there.

Verse 32 buries Joseph at Shechem, in the plot Jacob had bought. Genesis 50:26 says he was embalmed and put in a coffin in Egypt, and Exodus 13:19 has Moses carry that coffin out at the exodus. The book closes by putting him in the ground he was promised, in a field his family owned outright, after some four hundred years above it.

Verse 32 says Jacob bought the plot at Shechem for a hundred qesitah. The word appears three times in the whole Bible: here, at Genesis 33:19 for the same purchase, and at Job 42:11. What it weighed and what it bought are not known, and the Greek translators rendered it as lambs. What the verse does establish is that the ground Joseph is buried in was bought and paid for, not taken.

stories.keyTakeaway: Joshua assembles Israel at Shechem, recounts God's acts from Abraham through the conquest, and calls the people to choose between serving the LORD or foreign gods; they commit to serve the LORD, Joshua establishes a covenant and memorial stone, then dies at a hundred and ten.

intro:
Joshua was written by Joshua son of Nun, Moses' aide and successor, who composed the account of the conquest and settlement of Canaan during and shortly after the events themselves, c. 1406-1380 BC. Joshua himself records writing his words in the book of the Law of God. Jewish tradition holds that the closing verses recording Joshua's death at age 110 were added by Eleazar the high priest, with the note about Eleazar's own death added by Eleazar's son Phinehas. Joshua was born in Egypt during the period of slavery, came from the tribe of Ephraim, and served as Moses' personal attendant from his youth (Exodus 24:13, Numbers 11:28). He led the Israelite armies against the Amalekites shortly after the Exodus (Exodus 17), was one of the twelve spies Moses sent into Canaan, and along with Caleb was one of only two members of the Exodus generation permitted to enter the Promised Land. The historical setting is the Late Bronze Age, with Egypt's New Kingdom dominating from the south under Amenhotep III and his successors, the Hittite Empire expanding from the north, and the Canaanite city-states organized as a patchwork of small kingdoms loosely connected to Egypt through the Amarna correspondence.

Joshua is the sixth book of the Hebrew Bible and the first of the historical books in the Christian Old Testament ordering; in the Jewish canon it begins the section known as the Former Prophets (Nevi'im Rishonim). The Hebrew name Yehoshua means "Yahuah is salvation," the same name later borne in shortened form (Yeshua) by Jesus of Nazareth. Hebrew manuscript fragments of Joshua were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), with copies dating to the 2nd and 1st centuries BC.
